en: And thus, since the word *paṅkaja* has as its intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*) that which is delimited by the presence of lotus-ness (*padmatva*), there exists semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*) for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the agent of the production from mud— which is the object of the intention— and the lotus; therefore, it occurs [in the lotus].

Such is the resulting cognition of the relation (*anvaya*). However, where the sentence "There is a *paṅkaja* here" is uttered with the intention (*tātparya*) of referring specifically to a water-lily (*kumuda*),

since the existence of this thing in that place is sublated (*bādhita*) in the case of a lotus (*padma*), and because the determination of the speaker's intention exists only regarding the water-lily, the agent of the production from mud— which is the object of that intention— is [cognized] as the water-lily, not the lotus.

The sense is that because of the absence of the fitness [of the word] for denoting distinctness, existence, and so forth, there is no such understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) in that case. Now, even when there is a certainty of sublation regarding the conventional meaning of "lotus" (*padma*) in this region,
[the cognition arises] with the intention of referring to an object that is the agent of the production of mud-born things other than the lotus and the water-lily (*kumuda*).
Alternatively, if the intention were merely to convey the agency of producing lotuses, then the comprehension would be restricted to the *kumuda* (water-lily) alone;
since there would be no comprehension of the *kumuda* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in that case, the aforementioned text would be inconsistent.
Therefore, he completes the sense with "as a *kumuda*" (*kumudatvena*). By this, the contradiction is recognized.

The meaning is that this [phrase] serves as an indicator for the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Regarding the expression "another causal complex" (*sāmagryantara*): this reading is erroneous, because it would have been more appropriate to say "the absence of other causes. In this context, the word *sāmagrī* refers merely to the individual causes that constitute the causal complex.

It should be observed that the intermediate term (*antarapada*) refers to something other than the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*); furthermore, it should be understood that this cause is precisely the recollection of the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyarthasmaraṇa*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: in the case of a word with both etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍha*), it is not appropriate to accept a cognition such as "the lotus is non-different from the agent of arising from mud," because [the principle of] "that which is uttered once... [applies].

If it is argued that for this very reason there is a contradiction with logical principle (*nyāya*), such that in a case of both etymological (*yaugika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) meaning there is only the cognition of a single meaning— this is not so. For, just as there is a variety of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the cognition of the connection between two meanings— one etymological and one conventional— presented by a single word, so too is it in the case of etymological-conventional (*yogarūḍha*) usage.

The sense is that such a restriction of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is necessary. Regarding the phrase "but where" (*yatra tu*) in the root text, the meaning is "in whatever [word] delimited by a specific sequential order (*ekānupūrvī*).
By this, there is no defect even if the word *udbhid* differs due to a difference in pronunciation; for [the word] is what has been uttered...

The word "iti" is to be supplied as a remainder [of the sentence]. "Independently" means without making another object its domain. And this is stated for the purpose of excluding those words that possess both etymological and conventional meanings (yogarūḍha). In the root text, the phrase "even a particular sacrifice" refers to the *udbhid* [sacrifice].

The meaning is: "one who desires cattle should sacrifice," and so forth. The intention is that in such cases as "udbhid [are] trees, shrubs, etc.," the understanding is that trees, shrubs, and so on are the agents of breaking forth (*udbhedana*).

||81|| Regarding the term *jahatsvārthā*: by the etymological derivation *jahatsvārthā yayā* ("that by which one abandons its own primary meaning"), [it refers to the type of compound where the constituent members lose their individual meanings].

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is that which produces a verbal cognition whose object is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), while not having the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) as its object, as in the case of the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*) with respect to the riverbank (*tīra*). Here, the word *sva* refers to that which is intended to be the indicator;
the word *artha* refers to the denotable meaning. This should be understood likewise in what follows. In this very way, it is not [an indication] that abandons its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*).

By the etymological derivation "that by which one goes" (yayā yāti), it is *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning). In examples such as "the umbrella-bearers" (*cchatriṇaḥ*), the word "umbrella-bearer" generates a cognition of a group of travelers characterized by the presence of an umbrella-bearer;
thus, the meaning is that there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the state of being part of a single group characterized by an umbrella-bearer. Regarding the phrase "the first":
The meaning is "that which abandons its own primary sense" (*jahatsvārthā*). "Because of the lack of internal consistency that will be stated later" means:

since the basis for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*), there would be an inconsistency in the form of the impossibility of indicating the word "staffs" (*yaṣṭi*) as referring to "staff-bearers" in examples such as "Bring in the staffs. This is the meaning [of the phrase] in the root text.

"By being the bearer of a single caravan" (*ekasārthavāhitvena*): a "single caravan" (*ekaḥ sārthaḥ*) is a collective entity (*samudāyatva*), which consists in being the object of a cognition whose content is that [collection]. "By being its bearer" (*tadvāhitvena*) means by possessing that [property].

The meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*) is "delimitation" (*avacchinnatva*), and this is construed with the "definitional status" (*lakṣyatā*) within the referent of the term "definition" (*lakṣaṇā*).

It is to be understood that at the root [of the discussion], this very [definition] applies. The meaning is that if there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of the word "crow-foot" (*kākapada*) with respect to the mark for placing curd, and in the case of the word "umbrella-bearer" (*cchatrin*) with respect to the collection consisting of the umbrella,
then— according to the intention of the reading found in some manuscripts of the root text where it says "indication applies to the state of traveling in a single caravan"— [the definition holds].

He explains: "qualified by being a fellow traveler in one caravan. Now, it may be objected that the etymological definition provided in the root text for the word *cchatrī* (umbrella-bearer) is inconsistent; for in the sense of "one who possesses an umbrella" (*chatram asyāsti*), the form *cchatrī* is already established by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *-in* added after the word *cchatra*, and thus it consists of a combination of base and suffix (*prakṛti-pratyaya-samudāya*).

Since it is a sentence, and because indication (lakṣaṇā) is impossible in a sentence due to the absence of expressive power (śakti), he says "the one with an umbrella" (*cchatrī*), etc. This refers to the view of those who maintain that sentences possess indication; for according to the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), in a compound such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), there is [indication] in the sense of a person possessing the king's ownership, and in words such as *pācaka* ("cook") and *cchatrī* ("one with an umbrella").

The intention is that the expressive power (śakti) is admitted in cases such as "the cook" (*pākakartṛ*) or "the one related to the umbrella" (*chatrasambandhin*). Now, it may be objected that this view does not withstand scrutiny; for in a compound, while the word *puruṣa* denotes the person related to the king through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it denotes the person itself through its primary expressive power (*śakti*), resulting in the meaning "a person non-different from one related to the king."

In the case of a compound such as *bodhapāpau*, if one were to postulate an independent power (*svatantra-śakti*), then since the cognition of "one related to an umbrella" can be established by the word *chattram* (meaning "umbrella") and the suffix *-in* (meaning "related to"), which are both connected to the word *chattram*, there would be no reason to postulate a power for the form *chattrī* in the sense of "one related to an umbrella. Otherwise, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple powers for words that have no meaning.

Furthermore, it is not necessary to accept a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in compounds and the like; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usages as *ṛddhasya rājamātaṅgāḥ* ("the wealthy king's elephants"), for in that case,
the referent of the word *ṛddha* would have to be construed with the exclusion of royalty within the delimitor of the referential scope of the compound *rājamātaṅga*.

This is not possible, because of the rule that a word-meaning (padārtha) is construed with another word-meaning, but not with the delimitor of the word-meaning (padārthatāvacchedaka). However, if the word *rājan* itself has the king as its meaning,
then there is no obstacle whatsoever to the non-differentiated (abhedena) construction of the meaning of the word *ṛddha* within it.

It should not be argued that such an application is unavoidable; for since the word *rāja* (king) indicates (*lakṣaka*) "one related to a king," it is possible for the king to be the delimitor of the referential object (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), as only the delimitor of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) [can function in this way].

This is because the delimitor of the referent (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is also a delimitor of the meaning of the word (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). As for the absence of the cognition of the connection of another word-meaning with the umbrella-bearer and so forth in expressions such as *cchatrī* (the umbrella-bearer), it is because that which has undergone composition (*vṛtta*) does not admit a connection with a qualifier,
nor does that which is already connected with a qualifier undergo composition.

Because there is a lack of conviction that this [meaning] arises solely from another rule of linguistic usage (vyutpatti)—namely, the restriction that the meaning of a part of a complex formation (vṛtti), such as a compound, a primary derivative (kṛt), or a secondary derivative (taddhita), cannot be construed with another word-meaning—he says: "But in the Nyāya view...
In reality, even in cases such as *dāsaśātana* ("slaver-destroyer"), where it is a part of the meaning of a complex formation...

Since we observe that in expressions such as "the leaf of Caitra was cut by the arrows of Dāsa’s wife," there is a comprehension of the connection between Caitra and other entities— such as the state of being Caitra or the state of being the instrument of the arrows— through the relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*), it follows that the connection of those other entities with the subject through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*) is unestablished (*avyutpanna*).
Thus, this must necessarily be accepted.

And so, since there is no possibility of preventing the cognition of identity (abheda-anvaya) due to the absence of being presented by words with identical case-endings—which is the condition for the relation of identity—it follows that there is no harm even if one does not accept the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that "the word *vṛta* [is used] in the sense of [the agent] who has performed [an action]. Nor is there any problem in cases such as "Caitra’s father" (*caitrasya pitā*).

Since we observe the occurrence of the genitive case-meaning— namely, "being related to Caitra"— as qualifying the "causality" that constitutes the delimitor of the referent of the word *pitṛ* (father), one must necessarily accept that even in the case of a delimitor of a referent, the relation of another referent can only be through identity (*abheda*).
Otherwise, such a connection would be ungrammatical.
And it should not be argued that since such a relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) can be excluded simply by the absence of being presented by words with identical case-endings and so forth,

the postulation of a linguistic maxim (*vyutpatti*) such as "a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning" is also not necessary; for if that were the case, [the cognition] from expressions such as *gavi paśuḥ* ("the animal is in the cow") or *gauḥ* ("cow")...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition such as "the cow is that which possesses a tail, body-hair, and horns. However, in cases such as "Caitra’s father," since it is a matter of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that another word-meaning can be construed even with that which delimits the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of a relational term, there is no lack of explanatory adequacy regarding the resulting cognition. And a "relational term" (*sasaṃbandhika-pada*) is...

It should be understood that this [expression] gives rise to an expectancy for a fixed relation. Regarding the phrase "being in the same caravan" (*ekasārthavāhitva*), the meaning is "belonging to the same group" (*ekasamudāyatva*). Although the explanation could be maintained even by accepting a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *chatra* (umbrella) as referring to a group consisting of an umbrella-bearer, nevertheless, the suffix [is possible].

It should be understood that this was stated precisely because it is improper to abandon [the meaning] when it is meaningful. "In a single caravan" means "in a single aggregate. "By way of lack of expectancy" is used because it is unestablished in grammar for there to be a relation by identity (*abheda*) when the delimitors of the object-to-be-designated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) are one and the same.

The point is that there is an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the cognition of the relation [of the agent] as the substratum of the agency of going within that which is qualified by the agency of going. Regarding the phrase "and not": if the word *chatra* (umbrella) were to denote the aggregate consisting of the umbrella-bearer, then in the verbal cognition produced by it, the primary meaning in the form of the umbrella [would not appear].

It should be understood that this is because there is no appearance [of the meaning] as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*). Regarding the definition of a sentence (*vākyalakṣaṇa*): this is merely a superficial solution. In reality, even though the denoted object (*śakyārtha*) appears as a qualifier within the cognition produced by the word itself, it does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthatva*). For this very reason, in cases where the word *gaṅgā*...

The indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of being "on the bank of the Gaṅgā" is *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning). However, it should be noted that even according to the Nyāya school, where there is indication by way of being "the bank," that alone is *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning of its own meaning); thus, in cases such as "one with an umbrella" (*cchatrī*), the establishment of *ajahatsvārthā* indication must be understood accordingly. As for the phrase "by way of being the bank": this too...

It should be noted that the justification for *ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (indication without abandoning one's own primary meaning) even in the case of the word *chatra*—which indicates a collection formed by umbrellas—is based on its being a qualifier that conveys the cognition of an umbrella; this is indeed contradictory to what was stated previously.
As for the phrase "as the state of being a bank" (*tīratvena*), this too is likewise contradictory to what was stated previously.

It should be noted that since the word *chattrin* (umbrella-bearer) indicates the umbrella as a qualifier while signifying the aggregate (*samudāya*) formed by its connection with it, the theory of "non-abandonment of one's own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*) is applicable there as well; thus, the possibility of non-abandonment of one's own meaning exists even in that case. Furthermore, it is not the case that the word *chattrin* functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) merely as an aggregate.

It should not be argued that there is no contradiction between the preceding and subsequent passages because the objection regarding the incompatibility with the theory of *ajahatsvārtha* (non-abandonment of one's own meaning) was already raised earlier by the words "nor [is there a contradiction]... and so forth; for even so, the resolution remains that the theory of *ajahatsvārtha* is only tenable in cases where the word "umbrella" (*chatra*) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its being part of a collective group formed by umbrellas.

Alternatively, because it would be inappropriate to establish that [the word] does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*) according to the view of those who maintain that a sentence is characterized by a function (*vākya-lakṣaṇā*), for this very reason the author himself will state: "For it is universally accepted that the word *gaṅgā* has a 'meaning-abandoning' indication (*jahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā*) precisely where the word *gaṅgā* indicates [the bank] as a bank (*tīra-tvena*). For in that case:

Even when there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the greatness of every word as being the bank of the Gaṅgā, it appears that some accept the theory of "not abandoning one's own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthatva*). And that [theory] is only consistent with the view that "not abandoning one's own meaning" occurs precisely where there is a cognition of the connection between the denoted meaning and another word-meaning.

Thus it should be considered. Regarding the phrase "of the over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgasya*): the meaning is that if one were to admit the appearance in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) even of that which is not the object of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word through its function (*vṛtti*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a verbal cognition having cloth (*paṭa*) as its object could arise from a word such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*). And so it is.

The point is that by accepting the rule that "the recollection of the word-meaning has as its qualificandum precisely that which is delimited by the property [dharma] whose relation with the denotatum was grasped, and the verbal cognition likewise has as its qualificandum that which is delimited by that same property," there is no possibility of a verbal cognition regarding a cloth arising from words such as "jar. [This refers to the phrase] "of the relation with the flow [of water]."

And thus, the point is that because the relation with the primary meaning— which constitutes indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— is absent in "bankness" (*tīratva*), which is the delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), there is no indication [therein] either. Although the relation with the primary meaning in the form of "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) certainly exists in "bankness," nevertheless...

The intention of the authors of the treatises is that, because two simultaneous functions are contradictory, just as one cannot have two powers, one cannot likewise accept a verbal cognition of two word-meanings at once through two secondary indications (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, it is impossible for both "bankness" and "fishness" to be cognized from a single word [such as *gaṅgā*]. [For example: "In the Gaṅgā there are a hamlet and a fish."

However, if one accepts the validity of such usage [as "the Ganges flows"], it should be noted that there is no simultaneous verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding two distinct objects by means of two co-occurrent applications of the same word. Therefore, it should be understood that in the aforementioned instance, even though both the bank and the current are cognized from the word *gaṅgā* at one and the same time, there is no logical flaw. [End of] the root-text.
Regarding the phrase "But [nevertheless]," etc., the following should be noted here: if one does not accept the denotative power (śakti) in the delimiting factor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*),

there would arise the contingency of a verbal cognition from the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*) sometimes as "being a substance distinct from the eight substances," sometimes as "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*), and sometimes as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*).

Because it is possible to have a cognition of the expressive power (*śakti*) in the form: "The meaning denoted by the word 'earth' is either a substance distinct from the eight [standard] substances, or that which possesses odor," and because the cognition of the expressive power [of the word 'Ganges'] is [obstructed] by the apprehension of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*), namely: "The bank is the bank of the Ganges, or rather, it is that which possesses conjunction with the current."

Because they share the same security and risk (*tulyayogakṣematvāt*). And thus, there is no rule that a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must have as its object something delimited by some single property; likewise, there would be no such rule regarding the cognition of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*). If one were to accept that the power (*śakti*) resides in the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), [then the same principle would apply].
However, there is no rule that from the word "earth" (pṛthivī) there must be a verbal cognition specifically as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva);

likewise, there would be no such rule even regarding the cognition of the denotable object (śakyārtha). But if one accepts the presence of the primary power (śakti) in the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka), then the rule that from the word "earth" there is a verbal cognition specifically as "earth-ness" becomes logically tenable.

This is because the term *pṛthivī* (earth) possesses denotative power (*śakti*) only with respect to "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and the substance earth itself; and since it is possible to establish this through the rule that only the denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*) appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) by virtue of that denotative power;
and because, while it is accepted that the non-denoted (*alakṣya*) may appear in verbal cognition through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the object in question] does not appear through indication.

Indeed, a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) certainly occurs sometimes with respect to "bankness" and sometimes with respect to "Ganges-bankness. However, this point must be further considered here: it is accepted that the cause of verbal cognition is precisely the knowledge of the word-potency (śaktijñāna) which apprehends the delimitor of the denotatum (śakyatāvacchedakatva) as being the delimitor of the property-substratum (dharmitāvacchedaka).

Furthermore, the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is everywhere a property that is neither too narrow nor too wide (*laghv-nyūnānatiriktavṛtti*), because when a lighter [property] is possible, one does not accept a heavier [property] as being the delimitor in the sense of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*).

For this very reason, the cognition of the word-potency (*śakti*)— namely, "the earth is the denotation of the word 'earth'"— is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*), because the potency is delimited by "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*).

However, there is no substance distinct from the eight substances such as water and the rest that possesses such [denotative] power (*śakti*), because their heaviness (*gurutva*) precludes them from being the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatānavacchedakatvāt*). This is just as in the case of the relation of denotability (*śakyasaṃbandha*); for it is established by the experience of all people that there is the cognition: "The bank of the Gaṅgā is a portion of earth that is in contact with the stream. Thus, earth is the denotation of the word 'earth'.
Since it is universally accepted that validity belongs to cognition alone— and not to a substance distinct from the eight substances— that the same applies to the cognition of power (*śakti*),
it is established that the cognitions of power apprehend a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) consisting of a relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Such a delimiting function (*avacchedakatva*) of the denotative power (*śakti*) is indeed supported by valid cognition; for in the cognition "the jar does not exist," it is the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) alone that serves as the delimitant of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). And thus, even though there is no denotative power residing in the delimitant of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), from the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*), through the cognition of its denotative power—

There is a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) in which "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) is the qualifier. However, due to an error regarding the expressive power (śakti), there can also be a verbal cognition [of the object] by means of "possessing fragrance" (gandhavattva) and so forth. For this very reason, since it is possible for one who is mistaken to possess a knowledge of the expressive power even through the delimitation of "possessing fragrance," a path not previously investigated by others is being postulated.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that [the object] is presented. Through the power of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*), the recollection of the word *bhramara* arises from the word *dvirepha*.
And by means of that word-cognition consisting of recollection, there occurs the recollection of the specific insect as the referent.

The sense is that, according to the aforementioned method of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), it is improper to accept a *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication of the indicated) as a direct relationship from the word *dvirepha* itself through its primary power (*śakti*).
Now, [one might object]: "In that case, what becomes of the universally established traditional doctrine regarding the *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* in the word *dvirepha*?"
To the question "What is the process of transition?", he says: "by that which is indicated. This means by the word *bhramara* (bee), which is indicated by the word *dvirepha* (double-r).

"Indication" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the cognition consisting of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). The use of the form ending in *-ākāra* (i.e., *lakṣitena*) is intended to convey the sense found in such passages as: "The very act of meditative worship (*upāsana*) is performed [on that which] has arrived immediately after hearing [the teaching]. This is the underlying thought.

Regarding the term "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*): that from which a suffix is prescribed is the base (*prakṛti*). Its meaning is that which, through its function (*vṛtti*), is the object of the presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by it; this is because [the base] conveys its own meaning as being connected with that [suffix]. And the suffixes are: case-endings (*vibhakti*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and verbal endings (*ākhyāta*). Thus, by the word *dvirepha*— [The remainder of the sentence follows: —[the base *repha* is understood as the object of the presentation produced by the suffix, and thus the meaning of the whole is "that which has two bees" (*dvau rephau yasya saḥ*).*]

Since the word *bhramara* itself is present through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and not its referent, how could there be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the objecthood denoted by the case-ending? To avoid this inconsistency, one must resort to "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), which consists of an indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) whereby the two *ra*-phonemes— the primary meaning (*śakya*)— are related to the word they constitute, which in turn denotes [the bee].

The point is that it is necessary to accept such indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of bringing about the cognition of a "bee" from the word *dvirepha*. Regarding the statement in the root text, "it is not a producer [of experience]," the meaning is that it is not a generator of verbal experience (*śābdānubhava*).
Thus, the point is that in the case of an indicatory word, there is only a power of recollection (*smārikā-śakti*), and not a power of producing experience (*anubhāvikī*).

Now, one might object: "In that case, how can the meaning conveyed by indication (lākṣaṇika-artha) appear in verbal cognition? Anticipating this doubt, it is held that it is precisely another word possessing primary denotative power (śakta-pada), occurring in syntactic proximity with the indicated word, that serves as the cause for the cognition of its own meaning as related to the indicated meaning; thus, [the indicated meaning appears] through that very other word possessing primary denotative power.

He resolves [the objection] by stating that, since a word possessing secondary meaning (lākṣaṇika) serves as a cause for the cognition of its own meaning as connected with the meaning of another word, the manifestation of the secondary meaning in verbal cognition occurs through another word that possesses primary power (śakta)— namely, the other word possessing primary power that is co-occurrent (samabhivyāhṛta) with the word possessing secondary meaning.

He provides the resolution—namely, that the indirect (lakṣaṇika) meaning appears in verbal cognition through another word that possesses expressive power (*śakta*)—by stating: "of the indirect meaning.
This means: "because of the determination of capacity," that is, because of the determination of expressive power (*śakti*).

Since the phrase "the interval between the words situated at the base" has the meaning of being distinct from words that possess secondary signification (lakṣaṇika), it follows that even all words possessing primary power (śakti) would produce a verbal cognition of a secondarily signified meaning; however, this is incorrect.
For instance, in the sentence "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," it is only the word "hamlet" (ghoṣa) [that functions in such a way].

Since the capacity to generate a verbal cognition of the riverbank is established by the experience of everyone, he explains [the text] with the words "another word" (*padāntaram*). "Co-occurrent" (*samabhivyāhṛtam*) means co-occurrent with that word which possesses a secondary signification (*lākṣaṇika*). And thus...

The meaning is that a word possessing denotative power (*śakta*), when uttered in proximity with words having a secondary signified sense (*lakṣaṇika*), generates a verbal cognition whose object is the secondary signified sense (*lakṣyārtha*) recalled by that [word].
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the other words": this means the objects remembered as being produced by the other words.

(In this case, the meaning of the third case [instrumental] or the word *vaiśiṣṭya*—meaning "the state of being qualified"—conjoined with the knowledge having itself as its object, is connected to the other member of the compound.

Regarding the term *kumati*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose intellect (*mati*) is contemptible (*kutsitā*)," the latter member (*uttarapada*) has the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇikatayā*) of "possessing contemptible knowledge," while the former member...

In the case of the expression "kumatiḥ paśuḥ" (the dull-witted person is a beast), since the word *paśu* indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya*) through its function as a qualifier, it is devoid of its own primary meaning; furthermore, because the state of being a beast (*paśutva*) is sublated in the context of a dull-witted person, the word *paśu* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean one who resembles a beast.

Consequently, since there is no word here that possesses a primary denotative power (*śakta*), there would be no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in that instance. To this [objection], [it is replied]:...

The point is that for the sake of accounting for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), even in the case of a word used in its secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*), an experiential power (*ānubhāvikī śakti*) must necessarily be admitted. Regarding the example "the teacher’s family" (*gurukulam*) and so forth: the word "family" (*kulam*) is understood by way of apposition. In the expression "Caitra’s teacher," the relation to Caitra is construed with the quality of being a teacher (*gurutva*) itself.

Nor should it be argued that the relation to Caitra should be construed with the teacher alone; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of using such an expression even in reference to Caitra’s son and others, since Caitra’s son is also a teacher to someone and is related to Caitra—this is how it should be understood. Now, [an objection]:...

One might ask: since terms such as *guru* (teacher) are relational, it is possible for another word-meaning to be construed with a single part of that term's referent; however, since the word *nadī* (river) is not like that, how can the meaning of the word *gambhīra* (deep) be construed with a single part of its referent? To this, he says: "By means of a difference in words," because there is a difference in linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*).

"Due to the difference in expectancy. "The word under discussion" means the word *nadī* (river) occurring within this sentence. "'Only the subsequent word'—although the example 'gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ' (a hamlet on a deep river) was already cited previously, and in that case the locative case-ending is indeed heard after the word *gabhīra* as well..."

Although this [interpretation] is untenable, nevertheless, since the case-ending of the qualifier is everywhere devoid of meaning, it is improper to assume that it possesses meaning; furthermore, because the word "ghoṣa" (settlement) is not proximate to "gabhīrāyām" (in the deep), verbal cognition would be impossible,
and because it is entirely untenable in cases such as "gabhīra-nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ" (the settlement is in the deep river), such an assumption cannot be maintained.
This is the intended meaning. (Regarding the phrase "the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*":

the meaning is that it consists of the recollection of the primary referent (*śakyārtha*) of the word *gaṅgā*. The intended meaning is that the cognition produced by the sentence, however, is indeed verbal cognition [*śābdabodha*].
Regarding the phrase "of *gaṅgāyām* as well": this refers to the case in [the sentence] *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*.
The indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs in the word *gaṅgā* alone, as is accepted by all, and not in the sentence *gaṅgāyām*,
because there is no lack of semantic consistency (*anupapatti*) in the indication of the word. This is because even the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the sentence *gaṅgāyām*—
namely, "the [action] resides on the bank of the Gaṅgā"— has the Gaṅgā as its object, and thus possesses a relation to it.
The point is that because [the word "bank"] exists on the bank, even such a sentence would result in the bank being treated as having a secondary (lakṣaṇika) meaning.

And this was stated with the intention of referring to the apprehension of a relationship between the denotable object and the bank as "the bank of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgātīratva*). However, it should be noted that if [the relationship] were apprehended simply as "bank-ness" (*tīratva*), then the flowing current (*pravāha*) would not be the object of the cognition produced by the sentence.

Regarding the phrase "by way of reality" (*tattvena*): the intended meaning is that the relation of being the object of a cognition—which possesses a producedness (*janyatā*) determined by a generative capacity (*janakatā*) restricted by a particular sequence of phonemes (*ānupūrvī*)—is precisely what constitutes the denotation (*lakṣā*) of that which is restricted by such a sequence. And thus:

In the sequence beginning with "in the Gaṅgā," [the word "Gaṅgā"] is not the delimitor of the capacity to generate a verbal cognition; thus, there is no contingency of defining the sentence as a *lakṣaṇā*. Although, with respect to a verbal cognition in the form "residing on the bank of the Gaṅgā," it serves as the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)...
It is necessary that the cognition of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the word "Ganges" with the form of the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) be a cause [of verbal comprehension].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such a verbal comprehension occurring even when there is a cognition of the word "Ganges" followed by the seventh case-ending.
Nevertheless, it is precisely the cognition whose object is delimited by such a sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) that generates verbal comprehension.

The point is that [the cause] is not merely that which is delimited by such a sequence; therefore, there is no consequence of the sentence itself being the object of indication (lakṣaṇā). Nor does it follow from this that the cognition of the word alone is the cause of verbal comprehension, rather than the word itself.

It should not be argued that, because a cognition characterized by a producedness (janyatā) as defined by a generative capacity (janakatā) delimited by such a sequence [of phonemes] is unestablished, it is impossible for even a word to possess a secondary meaning (lākṣaṇikatva). This is because this statement is made with the intention that the word, insofar as it is being known, functions as the cause. [Objection: But what about in cases such as a verse composed by a mute person?
Since verbal cognition arises even in the absence of a word, this view is not tenable upon scrutiny; therefore,

it must necessarily be admitted that the definition (*lakṣaṇā*) of a linguistic item delimited by such a sequence of sounds consists precisely in its relation to the object of a cognition produced by knowledge delimited by such a sequence.

And since the word's being figurative (lākṣaṇikatva) is thus established exactly as it has come down [in tradition], he says: "Nor is it merely this much," and "delimited by thatness" (tattvāvaccchinna). "Thatness" (tatva) refers to such a sequence of phonemes (ānupūrvī); "delimited by that" means that which is delimited by it, namely, that which characterizes the deliminator residing in that [sequence]; [it is] delimited by the primary denotative power (śakti).

The meaning is as follows: that very thing which is the capacity to produce a cognition residing in knowledge, which is itself defined by a delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) residing in the power (śakti) delimited by the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā)—that is what [is meant]. And thus, the relation with the object of the cognition produced by the knowledge of power delimited by such a sequence (ānupūrvī) belongs to that which is delimited by that sequence.

The sense is that because the sentence terminates in [the denotation of] the *lakṣaṇā*, and because the sentence lacks [independent] expressive power (*śakti*), it is impossible for it to be indicative (*lakṣaka*). Now, if one were to argue: "Even in the absence of *śakti*, just as with a sentence, even corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are indeed accepted as being indicative," then he says: "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*).

"Non-occurrence of the definition" means that when the relation with the denotatum is grasped in respect to that which is delimited by *tīratva* (bankness), a verbal cognition arises whose object is delimited by pure *tīratva*; thus, the current (*pravāha*) is not the object of that verbal cognition—this is the intended meaning. "By the knowledge produced by itself," etc.

The meaning is "the recollection produced by itself. Although the exclusion of the sentence as a basis for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is possible even without the inclusion of the word "by its power" (*śaktyā*),
because it is only the word— not the sentence— that causes the recollection of the meaning, nevertheless,
when one recognizes the relationship between the sentence and the sentence-meaning as that of the signifier and the signified, the sentence also [becomes a factor].

Since it is possible for [the word] to cause the recollection of the sentence-meaning, if one accepts that the very relation between the object of the recollection produced by that [word] constitutes *lakṣaṇā*, then there would be no room for parsimony (*lāghava*) in defining *lakṣaṇā* as a relation with the primary meaning (*śakya*), because *lakṣaṇā* would not include the primary meaning itself. Therefore, the term "by means of the primary meaning" (*śaktyā*) has been introduced.

If one were to argue that there is indeed the burden of complexity due to the necessity of postulating a *tātparya* (intentional import) based on the requirement for the *paryāpti* (distributive relation) of each individual word, he says "moreover" (*kiñca*). Regarding the phrase "of the meanings of the names" (*nāmārthayoḥ*):
being the meaning of a name does not consist in being the object of a memory produced by the name through its *vṛtti* (semantic function); and a sentence is not...

How, then, can there be the cognition of the bank of a deep river through a name? If it is argued that— since a sentence consists of a collection of words, and since a collection is not distinct from its individual members—
the status of being produced by a name remains intact even for the recollection generated by a sentence, then [the same would apply] in that case as well.

It should not be argued that there is no inconsistency because even the state of being produced by a suffix (*pratyayajanyatva*) is unavoidable, and since it is possible for the bank of a deep river to be the meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the suffix can be construed with the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmārtha*) through a relation of difference. For if that were the case, [the following would occur]:

The point is that if one intends the cognition "the bank of a deep river," the application of the expression "deep river-bank" would result; for even those who maintain that a sentence possesses secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) cannot claim that such a cognition arises from the phrase "deep river-bank" alone, as this would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is the intended meaning.

"Because there is an absence of being a base (*prakṛti*) for the seventh [case-ending]" means that since the case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*) are prescribed only after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and because a base is precisely that which is the locus of the rule for suffixes, the definition "that which possesses meaning and is not a suffix or a root" prescribes the technical term *prātipadika* only for that which has a capacity distinct from suffixes and roots; thus, in the case of *gabhīrāyām*...
The point is that because the word *nadī* lacks the capacity to convey any [independent] meaning, it cannot function as the base (*prakṛti*) for the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*).

Nor should it be argued that, on these grounds, in expressions such as *nīlotpalam* or *pācakam*, the entire complex *pācaka-nīlotpala* and so forth— being sentences (*vākya*) and thus lacking the capacity to convey any [single] meaning— would fail to be the bases for their respective case-endings.

Because another rule, "kṛtaddhitasamāsāśca" (Pāṇini 1.2.46), prescribes that these [words ending in kṛt, taddhita, or compound] are also nominal stems (prātipadika), it is possible for words ending in kṛt, taddhita,

or compounds to serve as the base (prakṛti) for case-endings; in reality, however, they possess the status of being the meaning of the base (prakṛtyarthatva) through their linguistic function (vṛtti).

It is simply the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the *prakṛti*. And this [state] remains intact even in the case of "the bank of a deep river," which is the object of a cognition produced by a collection (*samudāya*) that includes the *prakṛti*;
for there is no purpose in including the condition of being produced solely by the cognizer (*pratyemātra*). [This applies to] Caitra’s...
Furthermore, in cases such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), since we observe the connection of the cow— related to Caitra— with the objecthood (*karmatva*) which is the meaning of the suffix,

it is impossible to include that [relation] [in the definition]. Moreover, even the property of being "determined by the base" (*prakṛti-nirūpitatva*) cannot be intended to be expressed in the *vṛtti*, according to the view of one who accepts the definition of a sentence as *lakṣaṇā*.

This definition appears superficially attractive because it is not established that [the word] *nīlotpala* and so forth are determined by their own respective *prakṛtis*. Regarding the phrase "having the same case-ending": the point is that in the expression *gabhīrāyāṃ nadyām*, the entire compound (*samudāya*) is not the *prakṛti* even of a single case-ending. Now, [the author continues:]

In expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man"), even though the word *rāja-* lacks a case-ending, we observe that the meaning of the word *rāja-*, which stands immediately before the word *puruṣa-* and is related to the king, is construed with the person (*puruṣa*) through identity (*abheda*). Therefore, in the present case as well, [the same applies] to the sentence ending in the locative case.

This [objection] is inconsistent, because there is no sublation (bādhaka) to the non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) of the meaning "bank" with "village" (*ghoṣa*), since the former occurs immediately prior to the latter; furthermore, being a word (*pada*)—

defined as that which possesses expressive power (*śakti*) while occurring immediately prior [to another element]— is also present in such a case for the purpose of generating that kind of comprehension of relation.

[Objection: It is the motivator (*prayojaka*). For instance, in cases such as "the color of a blue pot" (*nīlaghaṭarūpam*), although the string "blue-pot" (*nīlaghaṭa*) lacks the status of a word (*padatva*) because it is a sentence (*vākya*), we observe that its referent—the color related to the blue pot—is construed non-differently (*abhedena*) with the [property] of color (*rūpa*) and so forth. [Response: This is not so, because [in the case of] "a hamlet on the deep river" (*ghoṣo gabhīrāyāṃ nadyām*...).

It should be observed that since such a verbal cognition is established by experience even from a sentence, the impossibility of a cognition of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) therein remains as unshakeable as "adamantine glue" (*vajralepa*), because both the conditions of immediate antecedence (*avyavahitapūrvatva*) and identical case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*) are absent. Regarding the phrase "ghaṭaśūnyam" (pot-less): since the word *śūnya* signifies that which possesses an absence (*abhāva*), it is with respect to that very absence—a part of the referent—that there is a relation characterized by having a counter-positive delimited by pot-ness (*ghaṭatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*).

The sense is that this is because the relation of inherence (*anvaya*) is accepted [only] between a pot and its parts, not between a pot and a chariot. "Such a relation" means a relation of that kind. It is not accepted that one word-meaning is related to a portion of another word-meaning by way of identity (*tādātmya*), but it is accepted by way of the relation of difference (*bheda*).
Thus it follows: since there is no coreferential connection (*abhedānvaya*) of the referent of the word *citra* with the cow, which is a part of the referent of the compound *vrajapada*,

and because even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound there can be no coreferential connection of the referent of the word *citra* with the cow, which is a part of the referent of the word *go*, [the word *citra*]...
The point is that one must simply accept [the compound] as a conveyer of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Regarding the example in the root text, "ārūḍhavānara" (a monkey who has climbed up):

through the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "ārūḍho vānaro yam" (one upon whom a monkey has climbed), there arises the understanding that the monkey is the agent of the act of climbing whose object is [the person denoted by the compound]; thus, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound...

Since it is a rule that the understanding of an object characterized by a particular qualifier-qualified relationship arising from an analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is reversed in its qualifier-qualified relationship when arising from a compound sentence (*samāsavākya*),
one must therefore accept the understanding [from the compound] to be "the tree which is the object of the monkey's act of climbing."

If one accepts that the word *vānara* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "that which is performed by a monkey," and then accepts that the word *ārūḍha* has a secondary signification in the sense of "the act of mounting," this results in the fallacy of double secondary signification (*padadvaye lakṣaṇāpatti*).
This is because, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is held that secondary signification induced by the compound applies only to the final member (*uttarapada*).

The sense is that there would be a violation of the rule [of compound formation] and the rule regarding the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member; therefore, it is the word *vānara* alone that possesses the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the act of mounting by a monkey, while the word *ārūḍha* merely serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Now, an objection: the meaning of a mere particle cannot be construed with another nominal meaning through the relation of difference (*bheda*).

One might raise the objection: "Since the grammatical rule 'cādayo 'dravye nipātāḥ' prescribes the technical designation *nipāta* only for words such as *ca* and others that denote meanings distinct from substances (*adravya*), and since the word *iva* is not included among the group beginning with *ca*, [it cannot be a *nipāta*]."

He refutes [the objection] with the words "the term *nipāta*. The sense is that here the term *nipāta* signifies only an indeclinable (*avyaya*), since it is possible to obtain [the status of being a particle] for particles precisely because they are indeclinables. The phrase "without making the meaning of the suffix the medium" means "only by way of a relation distinct from the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*)."

One might object: "Has not the purpose of the phrases 'other than particles' (*nipātātirikta*) and 'by way of distinction' (*bhedena*) already been stated in the root text, but not that of the word 'directly' (*sākṣāt*)? Therefore, the word *sākṣāt* is redundant in this restrictive rule.
To dispel this doubt, he says: "on the ground," etc. [He adds] "even by the relation of being the locus" (*ādheyatā-saṃsargeṇāpi*). By the word "even" (*api*),...
There is a conjunction of the relation of the ground’s occurrence in the jar by way of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Regarding the phrase "because of the connection": although the matter is accounted for simply by accepting a cognition in which the mode is the ground’s occurrence in the jar, [the author argues that] by way of being the locus...

Furthermore, it is improper to accept that the ground (*bhūtala*) functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the jar, because it is not admitted that a category-entity (*padārtha*) can appear in the manner of a relation (*saṃsarga*). Nevertheless, following the cognition produced by the sentence "The jar is on the ground," [the doubt arises: "Is the jar located on the ground or not?"

Since the non-arising of doubt is also established by experience, there is a simplicity resulting from not having to postulate that the verbal causal complex (*śābdasāmagrī*) of that kind acts as an inhibitor with respect to a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) that apprehends a qualified object through its qualification— such as "the pot, which possesses the absence on the ground, is cognizable" (*bhūtalābhāvavān ghaṭaḥ prameyaḥ*). Consequently, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) [is admitted] even as a relation (*saṃsarga*).
The manifestation [of the cognition] is accepted as such.

If the cognition produced by such a sentence were of the form "the jar belongs to the ground" (*ghaṭo bhūtalīyaḥ*), then even the knowledge of the absence of the ground in the jar would indeed be a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*); thus, while the causal complex for the verbal cognition consisting of that [absence] is present...

The point is that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because, since the aforementioned perceptual causal complex— which includes a certainty (*nirṇaya*) regarding the qualifier of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*)— does not even exist, one need not postulate that such a verbal causal complex acts as an inhibitor for such a perception. This is the case in "The pot is not a cloth," where [the absence is] absolute (*atyantābhāva*).

The negative particle (*nañ*) cannot convey [mutual absence], because for the cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), the word expressing the locus (*anuyogin*) requires a locative case-suffix;
therefore, he states that the meaning of *nañ* is indeed mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)—namely, "the meaning of *nañ*" etc. [He says] "only by way of the meaning of the suffix."

The meaning is that [the relation] occurs solely through the connection with ownership (*svatva*) denoted by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the referent of the word "king" (*rāja*) is construed with ownership, and ownership alone is construed with the person (*puruṣa*), rather than the king and the person being construed with each other. The point is that in both cases, it is necessary to postulate a recollection (*smaraṇa*) concerning the sixth case. This is stated in the root-text (*mūla*).

Regarding the phrase "even for one who has not remembered the case-ending": although in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, by accepting a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of the prior member in a sense qualified by the meaning of the case-ending present in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) that qualifies its own primary meaning,
it follows that if that specific case-ending is not remembered, there can be no determination of the conventional metaphorical indication of the prior member in that specific sense.

Since it is impossible— because the existence of the knowledge of the form of the definition [of word-meaning] is precisely what prevents the recollection of the word-meaning produced by the word, and thus verbal cognition (śābdabodha) cannot occur at all— it is difficult to maintain that verbal cognition can arise from a case-ending that has not been recollected.

Nevertheless, even if the meaning of a conventional (nirūḍha) metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) cannot be determined without the recollection of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the general knowledge of that metaphorical indication and the recollection of the word-meaning dependent upon it are indeed possible.
There is no rule that the recollection of the word-meaning must arise solely from the knowledge of a conventional metaphorical indication; for if that were the case, [the following would occur]:
In cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the recollection of the bank from the word "Gaṅgā" would otherwise be untenable.

Thus, rather than postulating the recollection of various distinct case-endings in those instances, it is more reasonable to assume that the word "king" (*rāja*) presents its meaning through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as "one related to the king," and thereby accept a verbal cognition of non-difference (*abheda*).

This is because [the compound] is invoked due to its brevity (*lāghavāt*). However, in the case of the *karmadhāraya* "rājapuruṣaḥ," since there is an absence of the seeds for *lakṣaṇā* (such as the impossibility of syntactic connection), it is accepted that there is simply a cognition of the non-difference between the denoted meanings, namely, "a person non-different from a king. This is the intended meaning.
He states another opinion: "But others say... [He explains: "By way of the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti-vaicitryeṇa*)."

The meaning is that, with respect to a verbal cognition whose qualificand is a person (*puruṣa*), whose relation is self-ownership (*svatva*), and whose qualifier is a king (*rāja*), the knowledge of the word-order (*ānupūrvī*)—specifically, the state of the word "person" occurring immediately after the word "king"—is the cause. Thus, since it is possible to prevent such a relational cognition in cases like "the king [is] the person" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*) for this very reason, there is no room for the aforementioned undesirable consequence; this is the intended sense.

[The opponent argues: "There would be no reference (*parāmarśa*). [The author replies: There is a rule that by the word *tat*, there is reference only to the referent (*padārtha*) of the preceding sentence, and not to its delimitor (*tādr̥śapadarthatāvacchedaka*). Otherwise, there would result the natural usage: "This white pot exists; it is not a liquid. And so it is.

The point is that if the word *rājapada* (the word "king") were to signify a relation belonging to the king, there would be no coreferential reference (*parāmarśa*) to the king by means of that word. The phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates the presence of a lack of satisfaction (*asvarasa*). The seed of that [dissatisfaction] is that, if this were the case, one would have to accept a cognition characterized by the relation of ownership (*svatva*) even in instances such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).

This is appropriate; for the over-extension [of the definition] can be avoided simply by accepting that the knowledge of the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the genitive case-ending and the word "king" (*rāja*) is the determinant (*niyāmaka*) of such verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
Nor does this lead to a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the mutual verbal cognitions produced by the knowledge of expanded expressions (*vyāsa*) and compound expressions (*samāsa*).
It should not be said that causality itself is untenable;

for since the state of being immediately preceded by the knowledge of such a sequence must also be included within the definition of the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible. Otherwise, even in your own view, [the absence of] non-ownership by the king...

Therefore, in order to prevent such a verbal cognition [of "the king's man"] from arising from the word *puruṣa* alone, one must postulate that the cognition of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word ending in the genitive case is the cause of a verbal cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is "king-ownership" (*rājasvatva*); consequently, [such a cognition] would arise even from a sentence containing another synonymous term.

Because, due to the arising of such a verbal cognition, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is unavoidable; for if, in cases such as "the man is not [the property] of the king," the negative particle (*nañ*) were to convey only the absence of ownership and so forth in the capacity of a locus (*āśrayatā*),

since a relation that does not regulate the occurrence of a term (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*) cannot serve as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence.

If it is argued that the meaning of the case-ending must necessarily be "ownership" (*svatva*) and so forth— because it is impossible for the negative particle (*nañ*) to convey the absence of a king or similar entity through a relation such as ownership—

then what fault is there in a relation that does not restrict the function (*vṛtti-aniyāmaka-sambandha*) being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence?

Thus it should be stated. If it is argued that there is complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a distinct absence, we reply: no, because by accepting that such an absence is of the nature of the absence of possessing dust (*rajasvatva*), its name is unified with other co-extensive absences, and thus no further distinct absence is postulated. Nor is it the case that...
It should not be argued that there is complexity (gaurava) in postulating a counter-correlativity delimited by relations such as ownership (svatva).

For one must postulate a primary denotative power (śakti) for the case-endings in relation to ownership and the like; postulate that the mental representations of ownership and so forth produced by those case-endings are causes of verbal cognition (śābdabodha); and [postulate] that such representations are included within the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for the status of being an inhibitor of perception and other cognitions that have different objects.
Furthermore, considering the requirement for inclusion, it is simpler to postulate the existence of such a specific counter-positive (pratiyogitā-vyakti) itself.

However, this must be kept in mind here: according to the aforementioned sequence, the case-ending (vibhakti) would not have any meaning other than number. Moreover, regarding the word "rāja" (king) as relating to one connected with a king...

Since the cognition "a person non-different from one related to a king" arising from the *karmadhāraya* compound "rājapuruṣa"— which contains the word "king" used in such a figurative sense— is accepted by all during a state where the natural (non-figurative) indication is not grasped, [the cause] of such knowledge of the phonetic sequence (*ānupūrvī*)...

There is complexity in postulating that verbal cognition has two distinct types of causes. Furthermore, there is complexity in postulating that the causal complex for verbal cognition— comprising the knowledge of such a word-order— is an inhibitor with respect to a perceptual cognition that apprehends a qualified-qualificand relation (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*), such as "the person, who is distinct from one related to the king, is an object of knowledge" (*rāja-sambandhi-bhinnaḥ puruṣaḥ prameyaḥ*).

[This is] respectability. And in my view, at the time when the causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābda-sāmagrī*)—which consists of the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) and so forth—is present, there is no possibility of the occurrence of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the causal complex for perception—which consists of a determination (*nirṇaya*) having the qualifier of the delimitor of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka-prakāraka*)—is simply non-existent; therefore, such [a perception] is not postulated. Nor [can it be argued] by you that [the object is perceived] through the relation of selfhood (*svatva*).

It should not be argued that there is parity [between the two cases], because for the perception "the person possesses the absence of a king is an object of cognition" (*rājābhāvavān puruṣaḥ prameyaḥ*), one must postulate that such a verbal causal complex (*śābdasāmagrī*) is an inhibitor. [However, this is not required for] the perception "the object of cognition has a relation distinct from that belonging to a king" (*rājakīyabhinna-sambandhaḥ prameyaḥ*).

Furthermore, for one who maintains that "ownness" (*svatva*) is a relational adjunct (*saṃsarga*), it must be postulated that such a verbal causal complex (*śābdasāmagrī*) acts as an inhibitor; thus, the postulation of the aforementioned inhibition is more cumbersome in that view. Enough with this elaboration. As for the statement in the root text that there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a *dvandva* compound, that is not correct.

It is consistent. Since it is self-evident that in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) such as *ahinakula* ("snake and mongoose"), there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the final member with respect to the aggregate of the snake and the mongoose, he states—by means of the term "copulative" (*dvandva*)—that this refers specifically to the reciprocal copulative (*itaretara-dvandva*). [This is stated] in the root-text.

Regarding the phrase "in the manner of duality as the meaning of a case-ending" (*vibhaktyarthadvitvaprakāreṇa*), it should be understood that the meaning of the case-ending is "objecthood" (*karmatva*);

the sense is that the two objects, *dhava* and *khadira*, are cognized as being the qualifiers (*prakāra*) of that [objecthood]. As for the rule *supām* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], this cannot be sustained if one accepts the validity of the sentence "two ākāśas" (*ākāśau*).
It must be accepted that the number— characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to the delimitor of the objecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of the case-meaning such as duality—

is invariably construed with the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*) solely through a relation called "inherence" (*paryāpti*), which has itself as its nature. Otherwise, [there would be the absurdity] of the duality residing in both a jar and space [being attributed to the jar alone].

Because such a usage would result in being valid even with respect to space (*ākāśa*), since [the property] exists in space by way of both the relation called "mere pervasion" (*kevalaparyāpti*) and inherence (*samavāya*);
and thus, due to the non-establishment of duality (*dvitva*) as pervaded by the nature of space (*ākāśatva*), [there is no such property] in space by way of that aforementioned relation of pervasion.
Thus, there is no contingency of the aforementioned sentence lacking validity because it does not possess that [property]. And in this way,

the possession of that [property] by means of such a relation of pervasion (paryāpti) results precisely in the duality being pervaded by the delimitor of the scope of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka).

The meaning is that suffixes (*vibhakti*) produce a valid cognition of numbers such as duality (*dvitva*) which is pervaded by the delimitor of the object-to-be-indicated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). Because of the inclusion of the term "valid" (*pramā*), even though a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) may arise from a sentence such as "two skies" (*ākāśau*)— which, due to a delusion in a yogin, takes as its qualifier the duality residing in two pots within the sky— there is no [such production of a valid cognition].

There is no deficiency [in the definition]. Nor should it be argued that, since such a pervasion (paryāpti) is unestablished in the aforementioned case, how could an error (bhrama) apprehending it be possible; for, since the pervasion of oneness and so forth is pervaded by "space-ness" (ākāśatva), there can be an error regarding the duality residing in the jar and space through that extrinsic relation (vyadhikaraṇasaṃbandha).

Because [the dual number] is admitted to be a mode (*prakāra*). By this, it is shown that if the denotatum of the dual suffix were only duality as pervaded by the delimitor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-vyāpya-dvitva*),
then there would be no verbal cognition— even if it were of the nature of an error— from sentences such as "two skies" (*ākāśau*),
because duality pervaded by "skyness" (*ākāśatva*) is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

This has been refuted on the grounds that it is impossible for the case-ending (*vibhakti*) to convey that [specific meaning]. For, as explained above, the occurrence of such an error has been established. To claim that the verbal cognition of that kind arises through an error regarding the expressive power (*śakti*) of the case-ending as denoting mere duality is incorrect; for if that were the case, [the following would follow]...

It should be understood that the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by such a sentence cannot be considered erroneous, because the duality residing in the pot-space (*ghaṭākāśa*) is not sublated with respect to the [single] space (*ākāśa*) through relations such as *paryāpti* (inherence in a whole). In this context, [the sentence] "Caitra and Maitra go" [is cited].

It should be noted that in such instances, because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) conveys even duality and other properties that do not pervade the delimitor of the scope (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), such as "Caitra-ness," the term "of case-endings" (*vibhaktīnām*) was set aside and "of nominal suffixes" (*supām*) was stated instead. Furthermore, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*),
in cases such as "the jar and the cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭau*), duality is construed solely through the relation of total inherence (*paryāpti*).

It should not be argued that this is inconsistent because the phrase "in a case where there is a single property as the delimitor of the objecthood" (*supāmatya-traikadharma-uddeśyatāvacchedaka-sthale*) must be supplied [to complete the sense], since in the stated case two properties serve as the delimiters of the objecthood; for [this objection does not apply] in the final established view (*siddhānta*).
Even if that were the case, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, since it is the conjunction itself (*sāhitya*) that serves as the delimitor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*),

the addition [of the dual suffix] would not be necessary. However, in cases such as "the pot and the cloth remain" (*ghaṭapaṭau tiṣṭhataḥ*), it should be understood that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) does not convey number, because number is conveyed by the nominal suffix (*sup*) alone.

"Cocoonance" (*sahavṛttitvam*) means "subsistence in the same locus. "The characterized" (*lakṣyam*) refers to that which is delimited by the property of being the characterized (*lakṣyatāvacchedakam*).

"Co-inherence in a single action" (*ekakriyānvayitvam*) means "co-inherence in an object presented by a single expressive power" (*ekaśaktyupasthāpyārthānvayitvam*). Regarding the phrase "in the root, of those devoid of concomitance": this means "of *gotva* (cowness) and *aśvatva* (horseness)," etc. [In the case of] *gotva* and *aśvatva*...
In "paśya" (look) and similar cases, there is no impossibility of a *dvandva* compound because there is a connection with the action of seeing (*darśana*).

Therefore, he states another refutation regarding the second [example]—"paśya cchinhi" (look and cut)—even though the intention (*tātparya*) is respectively for seeing the *dhava* tree and cutting the *khadira* tree. This is because of the act of seeing.

The meaning is "because of the perception of a pair. With the intention that the objection—"because there is no experience of co-occurrence"—is also directed at the second alternative, he explains [the text] with the words "by way of the nature of things" (*vastugatyā*).
[He explains] "due to the absence of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhābhāvāt*); for it is indeed the state of being connected to a single action...
The point is that [the relation] is simply the state of being an object of verbal cognition as determined by a relationality which is itself determined by being the object of a single action;
and yet that [relationality] is not itself an object of verbal cognition, because one does not experience a thing having itself as its own object.
In reality, however, this is so even under the view that non-occurrent entities possess occurrence through the relation of time (kālika-sambandha).

In response to the very doubt that "the state of existing at one and the same time (*ekamahākālavṛttitva*) remains unimpaired, and thus there is no impossibility of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) anywhere," the refutation beginning with "of the coexistence" (*sāhityasya*) and so forth was stated. [This refers to] the [objection] regarding existing at the same time and so on.

We consider it reasonable that the meaning [of the term] is "because there is no experience of its being the object of verbal cognition. Regarding the phrase "by way of subsisting collectively" (*vyāsajyavṛttitayā*): although subsisting in a single part (*ekadeśavṛttitva*) and being connected with a single action (*ekakriyānvayitva*) are not themselves collective subsistence, nevertheless, in both positions...

The point is that, because of the statement of the refutation, "conjunction" (sāhitya) must be defined as being simply the state of being the object of a relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), and that [state] exists only as a distributed occurrence (vyāsajyavṛtti). However, this is merely superficial; for in cases such as "two are going," there is an application of the agency of going even by way of a duality that is distributed over both.
It should be understood that [the term] is used because it is accepted by all. Regarding the phrase "from a *karmadhāraya*":

the sense is that since there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in either of the two members of a *karmadhāraya*, the property of being a compound devoid of secondary signification is common to both *dvandva* and *karmadhāraya*. Regarding the word "conjunction" (*samuccaya*): [as in] "a jar..."

In the expression "and bring the cloth" (*paṭaṃ cānaya*), the meaning of *ca* is conjunction (*samuccaya*). In that case, because the pot and the cloth are dependent upon one another in their relation to the single action of bringing—which resides in the compound—there is no compound. Similarly, in the expression "wander for alms and bring the cow" (*bhikṣāmaṭa gāṃ cānaya*), the meaning of *ca* is secondary mention (*anvācaya*); here too, [the same principle applies] regarding the alms and the cow.

Precisely because it depends on an action that culminates in a compound (samāsaniṣṭhakriyā), there is a lack of syntactic independence (asāmarthya), and thus no compound [can be formed]. Rather, it is only in cases where there is the sense of mutual conjunction (itaretara) or collective aggregation (samāhāra)— such as *rāmaśca lakṣmaṇaśca* resulting in *rāmalakṣmaṇau*, or *ahiśca nakulaśca* resulting in *ahinakulam*— that [the rule applies].

The sense is that [this applies] to a compound (*samāsa*). However, the particle *ca* is employed only where there is a distinction between the word-meanings; thus, in the senses of conjunction (*samuccaya*), disjunctive addition (*anvācaya*), mutual association (*itaretara-yoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), the meaning of *ca* is indeed distinction. In that distinction, [the particle occurs] between the word-meanings being compounded in reality.

The meaning of the sūtra "dvandva" is that a *dvandva* compound occurs when [the members] are co-existent (*vartamāne*). Regarding the example "pramāṇa-prameya," etc., the intention is that since the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is non-different from the object of knowledge (*prameya*), a *dvandva* would not be possible there. And thus, in the case of "nīla-ghaṭayoḥ" (of the blue and the jar)...

Just as there is indication (lakṣaṇā) for the words "blue" and "pot" in the case of "blue-ness" and "pot-ness," so too in the aphorism beginning with "means of knowledge" (pramāṇa) and "object of knowledge" (prameya), there is indication of the word "means of knowledge" and so forth in respect to "the state of being a means of knowledge" (pramāṇatva) and so on;

and just as there is non-difference of the substratum in the case of the word "abhidhā," there is likewise [non-difference] in the case of the word "padārtha" in respect to the delimitor of the objecthood of the term (padārthatāvacchedaka).

Furthermore, since a word-meaning (*padārtha*) is that which serves as the object (*viṣaya*) of the cognition produced by a word, when there is a difference between two word-meanings—either between the two delimiters of the word-meaning (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) or between the two word-meanings themselves—a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is grammatically correct. In examples such as "the blue and the jar" (*nīlaghaṭayoḥ*), the correctness of the copulative compound arises precisely from the difference between the delimiters of the word-meanings. And it is not thus...
It must be explained how the difference between two word-meanings (*padārtha*) serves as the regulator for the grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) of a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

This is because it is accepted that the difference between word-meanings is the regulator of the correctness of a *dvandva* in order to justify the formation of *dvandva* in cases such as "the pot and the pot" (*ghaṭaśca ghaṭaśca*), which results in "two pots" (*ghaṭau*). Nor can it be argued that in such cases the rule "of similar forms, there is a single remainder" (*sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ*) applies.

Since the sūtra prescribes the elision of one member [of a compound] by means of another word, it must be said that there is no *dvandva* at all; thus, the effort to accept that the distinction between word-meanings (*padārtha-bheda*) is the regulator for the grammatical correctness of a *dvandva* is rendered unnecessary.

This is because the *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (the retention of a single form among identical words) functions as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *dvandva* compound, and therefore, the *dvandva* is only grammatically correct in cases where it is not superseded.
Since the rule for the *sarūpaikaśeṣa* (the retention of one among identical forms) must be applied,
and since there is no difference in the delimitor of the referent (*padārthatāvacchedaka*)— namely, "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*)—
in that case, the grammatical correctness of the *dvandva* compound is established precisely because of the difference between the two individual pots as referents.
The sense is that the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) based on similarity (*sarūpa*) which excludes those [other types] must be applied.

Nor, in this way, would there be the application of *dvandva* even in the case of a *karmadhāraya* such as *nīlaghaṭa*, because of the existence of a difference between the delimiters of the referents (*padārthatāvacchedaka*).

It should not be said that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the abolition of *karmadhāraya* compounds; for it must be understood that *karmadhāraya* is prescribed only when there is an intention to express the non-difference (*abheda*) between the meanings of the two words being compounded, whereas the rule for *dvandva* compounds is accepted precisely when such an intention to express non-difference is absent, since the specific (the former) sets aside the general (the latter).
