[Regarding the phrase] "uttered once" (*sakṛduccarita*):

This was stated in response to the objection that since a single word, when uttered once, conveys only a single meaning, it is impossible for the word "ghaṭa" to convey multiple jars at one time. Nor, however, does this render the rule *sarūpāṇām* (Pāṇini 1.2.64) redundant; for by the word "ghaṭa" alone— [The sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

In response to the objection that it is improper to prescribe the elision of a word after postulating another word based on the possibility of multiple jars being present, he says: "Because of the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).
[This is so] because of the difference between the delimiters of the referential properties (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), such as 'sūryatva' and 'siṃhatva', within the word *hari*."

The sense is that, because of the occurrence of a *dvandva* compound, the rule for *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (the retention of a single form) which serves as its exception would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Now, if one does not accept the etymological derivation "that which is uttered once" (*sakṛduccarita*), then from words such as *saindhava*, [the meaning would be understood] all at once...

The cognition of both salt and horse [would arise], because the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) is the regulating factor; nor should it be argued that there is no inconsistency [in this view].
For even when the intention is present, one does not experience the simultaneous cognition of both salt and horse.
To this, he says: "Let it be so. [Regarding the phrase] "a part of the word-meaning" (*padārthaikadeśe*): this refers to the meaning of the word *artha* in the expression *sakṛdartham*.
The meaning is understood through a function (*vṛtti*). When that function applies to a single part [of the meaning], there is a connection with the number one for the sense of "once" (*sakṛt*).
Thus, according to the etymological derivation, a word uttered once conveys its own denoted meaning through a single function.
The point is that the cognition of multiple jars is established by a single power delimited by the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*). Now, one might object:
in cases such as "The Haris stand," it is an empirical fact that there is a cognition of lions, the sun, and so forth when the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) is present;
thus, even in the case of words with multiple meanings, [multiple cognitions] occur simultaneously through multiple functions (*vṛtti*).
With the intention that it must be accepted as denoting multiple meanings, he says: "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*).

And thus, according to this established rule, the final meaning is that from the cognition of a single word there arises only a single verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), and not two successive verbal comprehensions.

This is the state of affairs. It is stated "and so forth" (*ādi*) because forms such as *ghaṭāḥ* are established by grammatical treatises as examples of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among similar items). "Cognitive apprehension of the collective" (*samāhārabodha*) means a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the objecthood (*karmatva*) expressed by the second case (*dvitīyā*) and whose qualifier is the collective (*samāhāra*).

"Because striking is impossible at the root. The meaning of the word "striking" (*vādana*) is an activity conducive to the conjunction that produces sound. It must be stated that the meaning of the accusative case—namely, the property of being the locus (*ādheyatva*)—is construed with the conjunction that delimits the meaning of the verbal root. [This is because] the presence of the conjunction in the intellect...

The sense is that [the definition] would be contradicted. Regarding the phrase "because of being literal" (anvarthatve): the meaning is that the designation of a collective (*samāhāra-saṃjñā*) is necessitated by its signifying a collection (*samāhāra*). Regarding the phrase "elsewhere":
the meaning is "in words that do not constitute a composite whole. This is because [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Because it would lead to the over-extension [of the rule] to the term *samāhāra*; because it is for the sake of the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word. That is, the refinement of a word such as *ahinakula* (a mongoose and a snake) consists in its specific property, namely its neuter gender and its being in the singular number; and [the rule] is for that purpose.
The meaning is that because it is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of that [formation], it is accepted as such only in the case of a collective *dvandva* (*samāhāra-dvandva*).

Regarding the term "virūpaikaśeṣa" (irregular single remainder): since the rule "sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ" prescribes a single remainder for words of identical phonetic sequence (*anupūrvī*), this refers to a situation involving words with different phonetic sequences.

By the rule beginning with "The word *pitṛ* [is elided] after *mātṛ*, *śvaśrū*, and *śvaśura*; [the words *bhrātṛ* and *putra* are elided] after *svasṛ* and *duhitṛ*," etc., the elision of the words *mātṛ*, *śvaśrū*, and so forth is prescribed;
in that case, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the couple who are the progenitors by the remaining word *pitṛ* alone.
When words are uttered together, it should be understood that the capacity to produce [a meaning] is perceived as belonging to those meanings themselves;
however, in their absence, it belongs to the speaker alone. Regarding the phrase "two fathers" (pitṛdvaya):
the point is that the referent of the word *pitṛ* (father) is precisely that which is delimited by the masculinity of a progenitor.

By the phrase "due to the absence of another way" (*gatyabhāvāt*), it is indicated that in cases such as the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) used in its primary sense, since the cognition of multiple pots is possible through a single instance of the word "pot," there is a way [of accounting for the plurality] even without resorting to secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
By the phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*), the lack of satisfaction with this alternative view is indicated. That is the seed.

Furthermore, there would be the experience of verbal cognition even for the word "mother" when it is not remembered, and there would be the complexity of postulating numerous distinct instances of memory. By other means of knowledge, such as inference (*anumāna*), one gains the knowledge that the word "brother" intends both brother and sister, and the knowledge that the word "son" [intends both son and daughter].
The meaning is: "and in the cognition that [the agent] is intent upon both the daughter and the son. This is a demonstration of the seed (bīja) for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*);

the sense is that the non-occurrence of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the seed of metaphorical indication. [The phrase] "established by the injunction to study" refers to [the qualification of the agent as] "one who desires [the fruit], one who is capable, and one who is learned," and so forth.

In demonstrating that eligibility for sacrifice belongs to one who possesses the materials required for the sacrifice, who is capable, and who possesses knowledge, it is shown that regarding knowledge, the Veda— defined as the sacred study (*svādhyāya*) which,
according to the scriptural injunction "the Veda is to be studied," generates the comprehension of purposeful meaning— is that which must be performed.

Since the attainment of knowledge is taught as being achieved solely through the study of the Vedas—given that they have this very purpose—and since the study of the Niṣāda is prohibited by the aforementioned scriptural injunction, the Niṣāda lacks the knowledge produced by Vedic study; consequently, his performance of sacrifice is impossible. In the absence of that possibility...

The sense is that even performing sacrifices for such persons is impossible. "Gaurava" means the burden of conceptual construction (kalpanā-gaurava). "Lāghava is ineffective" means that the parsimony resulting from not having to postulate figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is detrimental.

The point is that, because it would result in the invalidity of the aforementioned Vedic revelation (*śruti*), one must disregard even the parsimony [of the interpretation] regarding the connection of the literal meaning. Now, if by the prohibitive injunction "One should not harm any living beings" (*mā hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni*), all forms of injury (*hiṃsā*) were prohibited, then [in the case of] "A [sacrificial animal] for Vāyu... [the question arises...]

Just as in the injunction "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal," the force of the prescription for animal slaughter in the sacrifice leads one to accept that the aforementioned prohibitory rule is intended solely to prohibit violence other than that which is prescribed; so too here in the case of the term "niṣādasthapati."

Either the word "Śūdra" in prohibitive statements such as "women and Śūdras [are not entitled to study]" must be understood as referring to Śūdras other than Niṣādas, or else the meaning of the verbal root *adhi* preceded by the prefix *adhi-* (in the term *adhyayana*) must be accepted as signifying a study distinct from that which is useful for sacrifice (*yāga*).
He dispels the doubt that [the scripture] would lack authority regarding what is heard literally by stating "therein" (*tatra*).

By means of a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhāna*), the study that is thus obtained—namely, study other than that [already required]—is the intended meaning (*paryārtha*) of the stated scriptural passage. And so it is.

The sense is that, while the injunction "the Niṣāda chief" (niṣādasthapati) establishes for the Niṣāda the study of Vedic portions required for the sacrifice, the study of Vedic portions beyond that— and indeed the mere study of the Veda— is prohibited for all Śūdras.

Regarding the phrase "because it is not defective": one might object that in the case of *niṣādasthapati*, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in accepting it as a *karmadhāraya* compound; whereas in accepting it as a *tatpuruṣa*, there is complexity (*gaurava*) because one must assume that the word *niṣāda* possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to one who is related to the *niṣādas*. And thus, by way of injunction, for the *niṣāda*...

It has been argued that even if one assumes the study of the Niṣādas in accordance with the requirement of the sacrifice when it arises, there is no "burden of assumption" (kalpanā-gaurava), because a burden occurring as a result (phala-mukha-gaurava) is not a fault. However, this is incorrect; for since indication (lakṣaṇā) in the form of a possible relation is established by all [authorities], it is... [the rest of the sentence is cut off in the source].
"Because it is not to be conceptualized"—even if one accepts that this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is no additional complexity.

Therefore, having accepted it as a *karmadhāraya*, he raises the objection that the assumption of study for a *niṣāda* alone is burdened by complexity: "But surely... [He continues: even though the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is already established...

He raises an objection, stating "not so," on the grounds that the assumption of the cognition of that [word-meaning] as a cause for the verbal cognition produced by the Veda involves an unavoidable complexity (gaurava). This is because, in accordance with ordinary verbal cognition,
the cognition of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) has already been established as a cause for the verbal cognition whose object is the indicated meaning.

He provides the resolution— starting with "Of the Niṣādas"— by showing that since the verbal cognition of Vedic words is likewise accounted for in this very way, there is no need to postulate a separate causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the case of the Veda; thus,
even though there is no additional factor [in the form of] the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) as a cause, [the explanation holds].

The postulation of an infinite number of individual instances of verbal cognition produced by the Vedas— each of which would require knowledge of its own immediately preceding instance of cognition— is a burden that is indeed like an indelible mark (vajralepa). Nor can this be avoided by treating it as a case of knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in place of the knowledge of *śakti* (denotative power) established in their [the Mīmāṃsakas'] system.

He provides a thorough resolution by stating that "the nature of the relation to the denotatum" [is the cause], because the knowledge of the power (*śakti*) is necessary, and because the individual instances of the knowledge of that power are established for both parties prior to the verbal cognition produced by the Veda; and he says "not [denoted] by its own word."

A compound whose analysis (*vigraha*) consists solely of its own constituent words is called a "self-word analysis" (*svapadavigraha*); such a compound is designated as a "nityasamāsa" (invariably compound). It is precisely for the sake of establishing an analysis consisting of its own words alone that [this term is used].
The point is that this is because the optional nature of the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) has been accepted.

Regarding the phrase "having the meaning of the secondary member (*upapada*) as its qualificand": one might object that, if this were so, in expressions such as *upakumbhād āgataḥ* ("come from near the jar"), the connection of "nearness" (*samīpa*) with the meaning of the case-suffix—such as the status of being the source (*apādānatva*)—would not be possible; for suffixes [do not directly denote their own meanings].

It must be said that this follows from the rule that a stem necessarily conveys its own meaning as connected with the primary sense [of the suffix], because only the word *kumbha* occurring immediately after the *upapada* is the base (*prakṛti*) for the case-ending; for it is accepted that there is a difference in grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) corresponding to the difference between words. This applies to instances of compounds where the meaning of the preceding member is predominant.

The point is that, by accepting that the state of being immediately preceded and followed [by other words] for all such case-endings is what necessitates such verbal cognition, the aforementioned rule of word-formation (*vyutpatti*) is accepted as being restricted to such instances. Thus, it is the word *kumbha* itself that possesses the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "in the vicinity of the jar."

The *upapada* (the subordinate word) is that which indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Thus, some say that there is no need to assume a restriction even regarding the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*); he sets forth that view with the words "some, however," etc.
Regarding the phrase "near the jar" (*kumbhasamīpam*): although the word "jar" (*kumbha*) itself has the sense of "near the jar," [it does not follow that the suffix is redundant].
The claim that the form of the relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) is "near the jar," but that it is merely a recollection (*smaraṇa*) and not a relational cognition,
is inconsistent. Nevertheless, since there is a case-ending even after an indeclinable (*avyaya*),
if there is an intention to convey a cognition whose qualifier is the number of that [indeclinable's] referent, [one understands] "one thing near the jar."
The intended meaning is "verbal cognition" (*śābdabodha*). The phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates the manifestation of a lack of satisfaction (*akharasa*).

The reason for this is that, since an *upapada* (a secondary word) is never used outside of a compound, it is impossible to determine that an *upapada* has the sense of "proximity"; thus, even in cases where there is no analysis (*vigraha*) using separate words...

Furthermore, since the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is accepted by means of another word with the same meaning, it is more appropriate that the proximate word (*samīpapada*) signifies the object qualified by proximity, and thus the subordinate word (*upapada*) likewise signifies that very meaning;
for when it is possible for a word to possess meaning, it is improper to assume that some part of it is meaningless.

It must be considered: "the refutation of [the view that there is] denotative power (śakti). Although it was previously established that in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *rājapuruṣa*, there is indeed figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the prior member, and not that denotative power (*śakti*) was refuted in the *tatpuruṣa*;
even in the *tatpuruṣa* compound *ardhapippalī*, there is no figurative indication in the prior member, but rather in the subsequent member.
Thus, because this has now been stated, there is no room for the suspicion of redundancy. Furthermore,

since in various compound expressions the understanding of those respective qualified objects is established through either the primary power (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the constituent words of the compound, the existence of a separate power (*śakti*) in the compound itself is not postulated anywhere.

Because of the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*), the capacity [of the compound] in the mere aggregate will be refuted all at once; thus, there is no inconsistency. Nevertheless, the statement that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the prior member in a *tatpuruṣa* is for the purpose of refuting the capacity in the compound; by that very statement, it follows that in certain *tatpuruṣas*, [the meaning is obtained] solely through the indication of the subsequent member.

Since there is the possibility of a gain in that case as well—namely, that no postulation of a power (*śakti*) is required by virtue of the [text’s] completion—the suspicion of redundancy (*paunaruktya*) must somehow be justified.
Regarding the phrase "devoid of the *visarga*": because the word *āsatī* is without a case-ending (*nirvibhaktika*).

The sense is that, since it is possible for [the word *asat*] to be included within a compound, one can obtain the meaning "knowledge of the non-existent" (*asaj-jñāna*) by resorting to a *dvandva* compound for the sequence beginning with *asat* and ending with *tātparya*, and then adopting a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound for those [terms] with the word *jñāna*.
This is stated in the root verse: "But the proximity belongs to the word... (*sannidhānaṃ tu padasya*).
The literal meaning of the rule *copapadasānnidhyam āsattir iti* is understood as follows:

in that case, where two subordinate words (*upapada*) do not produce a mutual comprehension of their meanings, there arises the flaw of the non-existence of proximity (*sānnidhya*) between those two words; this flaw being evident, [the author] addresses that very point.

Demonstrating that the author’s own intended residence [of the work] is the seed for its etymological definition, he says "But surely" (*nanu*), and so forth. They [the commentators] explain the root text beginning with "In reality, proximity" (*vastutaḥ sannidhānam*) as follows:
when two words possess the capacity to generate a mutual understanding of syntactic connection (*parasparam anvaya-bodha*).

The intended meaning (*tātparya*) consists in the non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*) between those two words. Since that [non-intervention], being real in its own nature, is the cause of verbal cognition, it is established by experience that in cases such as "the mountain— [was] eaten" (*girir bhuktam*), verbal cognition occurs due to the delusion of non-intervention between the word "mountain" (*giri*) and the word "fire-possessing" (*agnimat*).

The denial of that [position] is a fallacy. Therefore, one must accept that the cognition of the non-intervention between those two words—which is common to both error and valid cognition—is itself the cause of verbal comprehension; thus, in order to examine that view:

The author of the *Mūla* presents [the objection]: "The counter-correlate of the relation," and so forth. "Relation" (*anvaya*) refers to the connection that has become the object of verbal cognition. The phrase "the word denoting its counter-correlate and its subcorrelate" means "the words signifying its counter-correlate and its subcorrelate."

He refutes this view with the words "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*). The meaning is that because [the cognition] is not required, there is no rule of necessity regarding the knowledge of non-intervention prior to the verbal comprehension.
Thus, the intended sense is that it is impossible to state that the aforementioned cognition is a cause, as its causal status is contradicted by instances of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) is unestablished;

for it is established by experience that when there is a cognition of the presentation of two word-meanings through two words without any intervention, verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) occurs even without a cognition of the non-intervention of the words.

[The author] explains non-existence according to his own view: "by the meaning of which word," etc. "The object of the intended meaning" means: the object of a certainty whose qualifier is the state of being the object of the intended meaning.
"Of those two such words" means: of the two cognitions of those two such words.

Regarding the term *tadupasthiti*: by the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) "the presentation (*upasthiti*) by that [word] is *tadupasthiti*," the meaning is "a presentation produced by a word qualified by such a non-existent [object]. This is because, according to the literal sense [of the previous definition], there would arise a contradiction with the preceding root-text, since the knowledge of non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*) is not required; and thus it is [interpreted] in this way.

The non-existence (*asati*) [of a temporal gap] between the two cognitions of the two words is precisely what constitutes proximity (*āsatti*). And that [proximity], being itself real in its own nature (*svarūpasat*), is the cause of verbal comprehension. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the previous root-text.
For this very reason, in the root-verse it is stated that "non-existence is fitness" (*yogyatā*), because *āsatti* is not included within the compound.

The explanation also fits well, because it is only when that [non-existence] is real in its own nature that it serves as the cause for verbal cognition. Nor does this contradict the subsequent root-text stating that "verbal cognition arises from an error regarding non-existence," since it is the *knowledge* of non-existence that is the cause of verbal cognition.

It should be understood that the phrase "due to error" (*bhramāt*) means "because the absence [of the object] is accounted for by error. This is because the aforementioned absence consists in the ascertainment of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), and thus, in the case of the connection between the referents of the words "blue" and "pot," since the speaker lacks such an intention, the absence there is accounted for solely by an error regarding that intention. Thus it should be noted. [The reason given is] "due to error."

The meaning is that [the non-existence of the word] is subsumed by error. It should be noted that when there is a certainty regarding the speaker’s intention that two words generate a mutual cognition of syntactic connection, the lack of intervention between those two words constitutes their non-existence;
thus, such a certainty regarding the intended object is of the nature of an error. Thus...

Even in the subsequent portion of the root-text, which states "even in the absence of a verbal error due to the absence of non-remembrance," the meaning must be described as "non-remembrance induced by an error," even when there is no verbal error (*śābdabhrama*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the context of the previously cited root-text. Regarding the phrase "of the nature of an error" (*bhramātmaka*), [it means] that whose essence (*ātman*) is constituted by an error.

The meaning is that, by the etymological derivation *svarūpam yasya* ("that which has its own form"), there would be a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by error; and this is merely a description of a positive state (*bhāva-varṇana*), because those two [negations] are absent in the present text.
Thus, in that case, there is a verbal cognition only of a non-existence (*asati*) produced by error, and not otherwise.
The sense is that the intention of the text is that even the absence [of proximity] is employed as a means of valid cognition (*pramā*). Regarding the verse:

the sense is that there, even when the words denoting the action and the factors of action (*kāraka*) are separated by another word, verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is established by experience. Regarding "non-separation of words": thus, the cognition of non-existence (*asati*) belongs precisely to that which follows immediately upon it.

We shall accept that [the knowledge of] the sentence-meaning is the cause [of verbal cognition]. However, it was stated "precisely for the purpose of dispelling the doubt" that [it is not the case] that the *āsatti* (proximity) existing in its own right (*svarūpasatī*) is the cause. Therefore, it should be noted that even if the author of the treatise were to admit that *āsatti* existing in its own right is the cause, there would be no inconsistency with this text.
Regarding the phrase "from the word [expressing] the action":

the meaning is that for the sake of establishing verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), it arises precisely from the word expressing the action or its factors (*kāraka*) that is uttered immediately [before];
for it is only through such immediate succession that this is possible.

The meaning is that if the two cognitions produced by the two words were separated [in time], it would be impossible for them to exist at the very moment immediately preceding the verbal cognition. By the phrase "so say," the lack of satisfaction with the view of the Neo-logicians (Navya-Naiyāyikas) is indicated; the reason for this is as follows:

Since [the causal theory] ultimately results in the view that the presence of the recollection of word-meanings produced by words is the sole cause, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the dissolution of "asatti" (proximity), which is universally established as a cause of verbal comprehension. Nor can it be argued that [proximity is unnecessary] because of the absence of words in cases such as the poetry of the silent sage.
It must be stated how there can be an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Even in the absence of an actual word, the knowledge of a word through inference is necessary;

otherwise, in the case of the poetry of the silent sage (*maunīśloka*) and the like, verbal comprehension would be impossible due to the absence of the cause, which is the knowledge of a word. And thus, for those two...

It should be understood that since the intention (*tātparya*) of the silent author is accepted as being directed toward the two words' capacity to generate a cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*),

and since inferential knowledge of those two exists without any interval, there is no inconsistency regarding verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) in the view of the author of the treatise. [The term] "non-difference" (*abheda*) [is used].

The meaning is that there is mutual non-difference among the individual instances of the recollection of the *tata* and *tataḥ* words. Thus, there arises a single recollection (*smaraṇa*) which takes as its object a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of those words.
The point is that from such a collective apprehension of the word-meanings, there follows the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the *tata* and *tataḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "having that as its qualificand," and so forth: since only a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) having a specific object as its qualificand and a specific property as its qualifier is the cause for a recollection having that same object as its qualificand and that same property as its qualifier,
a recollection arises that has as many objects as its qualificands and as many properties as its qualifiers.

Since only a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) that has that specific object as its qualificandum and that specific object as its qualifier can be the cause [of recollection], how could a recollection having multiple words as its objects arise from impressions that have individual words as their objects?

The underlying assumption is that the causal relationship between memory and its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is established solely through having the same objective referent (*samānaviśeṣyakatva*) and the same qualifier (*samānaprakārakatva*); however, this does not accord with the literal reading [of the text]. For if a memory has a certain object as its referent and a certain qualifier, [it must correspond to a corresponding impression].

Because there is no inconsistency due to the existence of specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) having that [object] as their qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and that [attribute] as their qualifier (*prakāra*); whereas in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no inconsistency because of the existence of specific latent impressions having that [object] as their qualificandum and that [attribute] as their qualifier, [there arises] recollection (*smaraṇa*) having that [object] as its qualificandum and that [attribute] as its qualifier.
The causality [of the impression] resides solely in its being an impression having that [object] as its qualificandum and that [property] as its qualifier;
however, for a recollection having those many objects as its qualificandum, only an impression having those many objects as its qualificandum is the cause.
Thus, there is no [need for] a single recollection in the form of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) arising from multiple impressions.

The core meaning is that there is no inconsistency. This is because there is an absence of sublation (*bādhaka*); the intention is that the recollection of the sentence produced by those respective mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) constitutes a single individual entity (*ekavyakti*).

Regarding the phrase "having various phonemes as its object": since a word is nothing other than a collection of phonemes, such a recollection of a word lacks an experience whose object is that very collection of phonemes.

The sense is that, since there is no latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the collection of phonemes as a whole due to the absence of such impressions, one must admit that the recollection of the word—having those many phonemes as its object—is produced by the impressions of each individual phoneme alone, functioning as a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*).

This is what should be noted here: although there is an "immediate contiguity" (*asatti*) consisting in the lack of intervention between the cognitions of the words that express the relata and the correlates of the relation (*saṃsarga*), [the recollection of the word does not arise from that].

There is no purpose in postulating that [the cognition of a word] generates verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Since verbal comprehension can arise through the presence of the cognition of two words by means of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of the word-meanings produced by them, it is impossible for the cognitions of two non-contiguous words to arise at the moment immediately preceding the verbal comprehension; therefore, [verbal comprehension does not arise] from those two cognitions of non-contiguous words.

Because it is impossible to produce verbal comprehension [from such a sequence]; for even if immediate precedence exists in the case of a non-existent [word], there is no purpose in postulating "unconditionedness" (*ananyathāsiddhatva*). Nevertheless, in a case where first there is the cognition of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), and then the cognition of the word "cloth" (*paṭa*), at the subsequent moment...

There arises a collective recollection (*samūhālambana-smṛti*) directed toward the word "white" through the cooperation of another stimulant (*udbodhaka*), which has as its object the meaning in the form of a jar produced by the cognition of the word "jar";
from that follows the recollection of the referent of the word "white," [in the form] "the jar is white."

There is no fault [in our position], because it is necessary to postulate that the aforementioned non-existence (*asati*) is a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), in order to prevent the undesirable consequence of such a cognition occurring [inappropriately].
He introduces the passage beginning with "But... (*paraṃ tu*) as follows: "Of those things which perish very rapidly," and so forth.

Thinking that there is a syntactical inconsistency in the root text of the verse beginning with "some... old men, young men," etc., which follows immediately after [the previous statement], he completes it with the words "they said," and so forth. Regarding the word *cira*:
the first-mentioned object is compared to the old man, and the second-mentioned object is compared to the youth.
The intended meaning is that there is a similarity with what was stated regarding "proximity" (*sannidhi*). Regarding the phrase "its own object" (*svārtha*) and so forth:

its own [word] is a term such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*); its object is the pot and so forth; that which is required by it is the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), namely, "Of what is this [the pot]?"—an object that arises from the mental presence (*upasthiti*) of that [object].
Proximity (*sannidhāna*), which depends on the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) because it is an object of action (*karmatva*),
attains the status of being the object of a collective recollection (*samūhālambanasmṛti*) whose content is the referent in the form of a jar.
Consequently, the own-meaning (*svārtha*) such as a jar, which is understood by the words "jar" and so forth, is construed with that [proximity] by way of its being an object of action and so on.
The meaning of the verse is that it becomes the object of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by that [sentence]; this is the intended sense.

By the word "first," it is indicated that the verbal cognition—that the potness is the object (*karmatā*)—occurs via the word "pot" even prior to the presentation of the meaning consisting of the act of bringing. "And subsequently" [refers to the following].
The meaning is: "after the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) whose object is the meaning of the constituent parts.

From the statement in the root text that "the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence (mahāvākyārthabodha) occurs," it should be understood that the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence does not occur immediately after the presentation of the meanings of the individual words (pādārtha).

"In the same way at the root, by the recollection of the word-meaning" means precisely by the recollection of the word-meaning such as "bringing," which is produced by the cognition of the word. He reveals the lack of satisfaction in the view of the ancients with the words "if this were so" (*evaṃ ceti*). [He states] "the final word-meaning."
The meaning is: at the time of recollecting the referents (padārtha) whose forms are "bringing" (*ānayana*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to destruction":

immediately after the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the pot and the objecthood (*karmatva*), there arises the cognition of the meaning of the partial sentence (*khaṇḍavākyārtha*) as "the objecthood belonging to the pot. Immediately after that, there occurs the cognition of the words "bringing" and so forth. Immediately after that...

The meaning is that, by the very process of recollecting the word-meanings, at that time the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the previously [cognized] jar and so forth is destroyed due to the recollection of the meaning of the word "bring. "By way of the presentation of the word-meaning" means "by way of the cognition of the word-meaning."

The meaning is "after the verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning of the subordinate clauses. From the statement in the root-text that "the cognition of the meaning of the major sentence occurs," it should be understood that the cognition of the meaning of the major sentence does not occur immediately after the presentation of the word-meanings. It is exactly so in the root-text.

The phrase "by the recollection of the word-meaning" means precisely by the recollection of the word-meaning, such as "bringing," which is produced by the cognition of the word. He reveals the lack of satisfaction in the view of the earlier [author] with the words "if this were so. The phrase "at the time of the final word-meaning" means at the time of the recollection of the word-meaning in the form of "bringing" and so forth. The word "due to destruction" refers to [the destruction of the cognition] immediately after the presentation of the pot and its objecthood.
The meaning is as follows: first, there is the understanding of the sentence-meaning as "the action of bringing the jar" (*ghaṭīyākarmatā*);
immediately after that, there is the cognition of the word "bringing" (*ānayana*) and so forth; and immediately after that, there is the recollection of the word-meanings.
It is by this very sequence—through the recollection of the word-meaning "bringing"—that the prior presentation (*upasthiti*) of the jar and other objects at that time is destroyed.
"By way of the presentation of word-meanings" (padārthopasthititvena) means "by way of the cognition of word-meanings" (padārthajñānatvena).

The intention is that even the verbal comprehension of the meaning of a fragmentary sentence (*khaṇḍavākyārtha*) is produced by words. Indeed, if the reading were "by way of the presentation of word-meanings produced by words" (*padajanyapadārthopasthititvena*), then the word *upasthiti* would have the sense of "recollection" (*smṛti*) alone.

"Common to verbal cognition" (śābdabodhasādhāraṇa) means that which is concomitant with verbal cognitions whose objects are the meanings of partial sentences. "By way of being such an apprehension" (tādṛśopasthititvenaiva) means by way of being a cognition produced by a word (padajanyajñānatvenaiva). And thus:

The sense is that, depending on the case, the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is either a verbal understanding produced by words or a recollection produced by words, both being characterized as knowledge generated by words. According to this view, he establishes that the comprehension of the meaning of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) involves the apprehension of a qualified qualifier (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*), starting with the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The word "where" (*yatra*) [refers to the following].

In a case where, after the comprehension of the meaning of a subordinate sentence (*khaṇḍavākyārtha*), there occurs the recollection of the final word, followed by the recollection of its meaning, and then the comprehension of the meaning of the major sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*),

at the time of the recollection of the meaning of the final word, the verbal comprehension of the subordinate sentence-meaning has already perished; therefore, it is only the recollection of the meaning of the final word that exists.
It must be accepted as being of the nature of a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) whose objects are the meanings of the individual sentences. However,

in cases where the recollection that generates the verbal cognition of the individual sentence-meanings is itself of the nature of a collective cognition having the final word as its object, it is precisely there— at the moment prior to the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence— that [the understanding arises].

The sense is that there is the existence of a verbal cognition whose object is the meaning of a partial sentence (*khaṇḍavākyārtha*). And thus, if one accepts the arising of a verbal cognition that apprehends a qualified relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*) by means of a collective recollection (*samūhalambanasmaraṇa*), even without a verbal cognition whose object is the meaning of a partial sentence, then in a case where...
Whenever, due to some deficiency in the causal factors, there is no verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding the meaning of the sentence as a whole,

but rather only a collective recollection (samūhālambana-smaraṇa) of the word-meanings, in that case the causal complex for the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence remains intact according to the principle of "the qualifier [is related] to the qualificand" (viśeṣye viśeṣaṇam).

He states that, in such a manner, the comprehension of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) is unavoidable, beginning with the words "In this regard, this is to be understood," and so forth. As for the phrase "the details elsewhere": just as perception and the other means of knowledge take the form of a "qualified-qualifier" relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*) according to the maxim "the qualifier [is related] to the qualificandum," so too [does the comprehension of the Great Sentence].

The meaning is that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) also [arises], because the presence or absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is equal in both cases. In the root text, the author refutes the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) with the words "by this" (*etena*), and so forth. [Verbal cognition arises] precisely through the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the final phoneme, which has been awakened by the awakening factor (*udbodhaka*) consisting of the experience of the final phoneme accompanied by the impressions generated by the experiences of the preceding phonemes.
The meaning is: because it has been established that there is a recollection of the word (*pada*) having as its object those successive phonemes (*varṇa*).
"By that very manifester" means: by that very manifester of the *sphoṭa*.
Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) maintain that the *sphoṭa* alone is the bringer of the presentation of objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), etc., [and not the phonemes]. Of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa-pada*)...
Since a sequence consisting of four successive phonemes can never exist simultaneously, it is impossible for it to bring about the presentation of meaning;

however, the *sphoṭa* is not distinct from Brahman itself as a category of reality, and although it is unitary, its manifestation through various individual phonemes serves to present their respective meanings.
At the time of the utterance of the word "jar," there is no contingency of the manifestation of a cloth or other objects.

Furthermore, even the conventional distinction between *pada-sphoṭa* (word-potential) and *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-potential) arises solely from the difference between the manifestation produced by a word and the manifestation produced by a sentence. And in this regard:

A word's capacity to convey meaning consists precisely in its being the object of a cognition that generates the comprehension of that meaning; and this [capacity] arises from a collective recollection (*samūhālambana-smṛti*) directed toward all those letters in their sequential order, following the experience of the final letter, even though the letters are multiple.

Since the recollection of the object, the form of the jar, leads to the arising of a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding the jar, it is indeed established that the word— consisting of a collection of phonemes— is the conveyor of the meaning "jar. Why then should the capacity to generate the verbal cognition of a jar be attributed by you to the *sphoṭa*,
when even you must admit such an experience of the final phoneme for the sake of manifesting the *sphoṭa*?
It must be accepted as a whole and not individually;
for if it were so, the meaning would result from each individual letter, and since letters are impermanent,
a collection serving as the locus of fulfillment would never exist.

They argue that since the capacity to denote meaning (*vācakatā*) cannot be fully realized within a word (*pada*) consisting of a sequential collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), it must be accepted that only the "stable word-sphoṭa" (*sthirapadasphoṭa*) possesses the denotative power for each respective meaning. However, even this is not capable of withstanding scrutiny; for denotative power is inherent (*samaveta*).
It is not a fallacy to say that the collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) is its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); for,
since an inherent cause must exist at the time of the effect in order to function as a cause,
denotative capacity cannot reside in a collection of sequential phonemes.
It would be untenable to claim that [the word] deserves to arise through inherence (*samavāya*),
because a collection does not exist at a single moment; rather,
it is simply the object of the Lord’s will by virtue of its being the generator of a cognition regarding those respective meanings.
The capacity to denote a particular meaning belongs to that [word]. And this capacity is indeed possible even in the case of successive phonemes.

Nor is the capacity to denote a particular meaning merely the state of being the object of a cognition produced by that [word]; for that is indeed possible even in the case of successive phonemes. It is not the case that [the capacity] consists in [the idea]: "from this word, this meaning is to be understood."

Because the Naiyāyika accepts that the nature of being expressive consists either in the will of the Blessed One or in not being its object, and because in that case "being produced" is the meaning of the fifth case (ablative) with respect to the collection of phonemes.
It must be stated that because God’s will is also non-existent in the moment immediately preceding the effect in the form of cognition, it would result in a lack of correspondence;

therefore, the meaning of the phrase "from this word" (*asmācchabdāt*) must be explained as "from the *sphoṭa* manifested by this word. This is because, according to the view of the Neo-Naiyāyikas (*navya*), a word does not produce the comprehension of its meaning [on its own].

This is because it must be accepted that the meaning of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is precisely "being produced by a cognition. In reality, however, a collection of phonemes does not possess the status of being a word; rather, it is each preceding phoneme in relation to the final phoneme that does.
And for that [final phoneme], it is indeed possible for it to exist in the moment immediately preceding the effect, which is the cognition [of the word].
Not even a scent of an inconsistency arises; for it is stated "by that very [cognition] which manifests it at the root.

This means: by that which you intend to be its manifestor—namely, the experience of the final phoneme accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experiences of each preceding phoneme—which is precisely what the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*) accept as the manifestor of the *sphoṭa*.
"Upapateḥ" means "because of the possibility of the recollection of a word consisting of a collection of phonemes.

The underlying sense is that we must accept precisely those [phonemes] which you yourself admit to be the manifestors of the *sphoṭa*, as being the exciters (*udbodhakas*) of the latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) pertaining to the entire range of meanings.

"But not by way of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*). This means that, according to the method previously stated, there is a recollection of the meanings of the individual words in the sentence, which has as its objects all the word-meanings produced by the recollection of the words "samūha" and "ālambana. Now, if this is so—

How could a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding a particular word-meaning arise without a recollection (*smaraṇa*) of that specific word-meaning produced by that specific word? For there is no recollection of the meaning of a complex sentence (*khaṇḍavākya*) that is produced by its constituent words. To this, he says:
"Not indeed" (*na hi*). In the root text, it is stated that the recollection of the word-meaning produced by the word is the cause of that verbal cognition.

It has been stated that word-supplementation (*padādhyāhāra*) is necessary because, without the knowledge of the word "close" (*pidhehi*), a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding the act of closing would be impossible due to its being the cause [of such a cognition]. That is not tenable; for, by parsimony (*lāghava*), [the cause] is simply the presence of the object denoted by the word (*padārthopasthiti*).

Because they accept that [the presence of] the mere apprehension of word-meanings is the cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), he states their position as follows: "of the mere apprehension of word-meanings.
For the Prābhākaras, it is sufficient that there exists the apprehension of some word-meaning whatsoever.
Verbal cognition is accepted as arising from the recollection of word-meanings produced by words accompanied by that [recollection];

however, verbal cognition is not accepted as occurring even without the knowledge of some particular word. And if this [recollection] were the cause of verbal cognition merely by virtue of being the presentation of a word-meaning, then for those [meanings] presented through perception and other means—

The sense is that the intention of the root text is that, otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of verbal cognition occurring even without the knowledge of the words for the meanings of those [constituent] parts.

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of *tātparya*": since it is accepted that the knowledge of *tātparya* is also a cause of verbal cognition, [the author] specifies that it is only the speaker’s intention (*vaktṛ-icchā*) [that constitutes *tātparya*].
The sense is that because it consists of intention (*tātparya*), if even a single word is not uttered, the intention— which is of the nature of the speaker’s desire— cannot possibly exist at all.
This applies to the case where some word or other is uttered.
He states— beginning with "But when that exists," etc.— that even the verbal cognition whose object is another meaning supplied by implication arises from that very [sentence].

Now, if a word denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) were to generate verbal cognition without a verb, then in the case of the sentence "The door, the closing, the effort," [it would also follow].

Since it would follow that there could be no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) concerning the action performed in accordance with the closing of the door, one must accept that a word expressing a *kāraka* (participant in an action) cannot produce verbal cognition without a verb (*kriyāpada*).
Consequently, the insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of a verb is necessary; thus, the intention of the root text beginning with "kiñca" and so forth is not tenable.
When "door" is uttered,
for those who accept that there is a verbal cognition regarding the closing [of the door] and so forth— which are presented through perception and other means—

even from a word whose expectancy has been satisfied, it is possible to admit the desired verbal cognition regarding the closing and so forth that have been presented; therefore, the intention (*tātparya*) is restricted [to the specific relation].
He describes it as "the door. Thus, even when there is *tātparya* (intentional meaning),
since verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is contrary to experience in cases where all words are present but lack mutual expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*),
[the word] "door" [is required] for the verbal cognition of an effort conducive to the closing of the door.

Since it is necessary for the knowledge of word-order (*ānupūrvī*) to be the cause [of verbal cognition], if a verb is not supplied (*anadhyāhāra*), the absence of such knowledge of word-order would render the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) untenable; therefore, the supply of a verb (*kriyāpadādhyāhāra*) is indispensable.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the passage beginning with "he becomes angry" (*krudhyati*), since the rule prescribes the technical designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) for that person toward whom the anger is directed when used in conjunction with verbal roots meaning "to be angry," "to hate," "to envy," or "to be malicious," and since the dative case is prescribed for the *saṃpradāna*, this is the intended sense.
Regarding the phrase "by the grammatical instruction" (*anuśāsanena*), it refers to the object of desire in connection with the root *spṛh* (to desire).

The intention is that [the dative case] is prescribed by the rule defining the technical term *saṃpradāna*. However, when used in conjunction with a verbal root meaning "to desire," only the accusative case after words such as *puṣpa* (flower) is correct, and not the dative;

for in that construction, the object of the desire is not assigned the technical term *saṃpradāna*. Therefore, in order to justify the correctness of the dative case, [one must resort to the following].
The collective purport [of the commentary] is that the ellipsis of the word *spṛhayati* is necessary.
"In some cases" means in instances such as *puṣpebhyaḥ*,
for the purpose of establishing the grammatical correctness of the dative case.

The meaning is that one should supply words such as "spṛhayati" (he desires). Regarding the phrase "by way of being a presentation produced by that": it means by way of being a presentation produced by verbal roots such as *spṛh* and so on. Regarding the phrase "not being a cause of verbal cognition": [this is] because of parsimony (*lāghava*), [it is established] that [the word-meaning] is a cause for verbal cognition in general alone.

The point is that since the cause [of verbal comprehension] is determined to be simply the "presence of the word-meaning" (*padārthopasthiti*), it follows that in cases such as "the door," the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of words like "close" (*pidhehi*) is not necessary. Furthermore, this is the final point: even when the expression "perform the closing" (*pidhānaṃ kuru*) is used, the accusative case in "the door" (*dvāram*) would not [be required].

This is correct; for by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, the genitive case is replaced by the accusative because [the agent] is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the capacity to produce [the action]. Thus, in cases such as *dvāram* ("the door"), since there is no obstacle to the cognition of "closing" (*pidhāna*) and so forth—which are somehow brought to mind—the position of supplying the meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*) is justified.

Regarding the term "evocita" (appropriate): in the root text, by the statement "in that case, the fitness [of one thing] with respect to the object [denoted by] the word is proclaimed," it is said that the fitness [of a word] with respect to a particular object is its possession of that object;
however, this is both incorrect and useless, because a thing cannot have itself as its own locus.

And because the knowledge of that [word] lacks causality with respect to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), he explains [the text] with the intention that the first occurrence of the word *tat* refers to the meaning of one word, while the second occurrence of the word *tat* refers to the meaning of the other word: "the meaning of one word" (*ekapadārtha*).
He states the proof for the fact that the knowledge of fitness (*yogyatājñāna*) is a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) with the words "and because of the absence of the knowledge thereof.
"Because of its being unprecedented" (*apūrvatvāt*) means that it has not been ascertained prior to every instance of verbal comprehension. "In some cases, of doubt" (*kvacit saṃśayasya*)...
The meaning is that [the cause] is the cognition of fitness (yogyatā) insofar as it is common to both doubt and certainty.

For this very reason, he also shows certainty with the words "in some cases" (kvacit). This means that in the case of a verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) occurring subsequent to a perceptual certainty such as "there is a jar on the ground."

The Navyas, however, say: "But surely, if the certainty of unfitness (*ayogyatāniścaya*) is an impediment, then its absence must be stated as the cause [of verbal comprehension]. Since it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to hold that the knowledge of fitness (*yogyatājñāna*) itself is the cause rather than that, he says: 'of the certainty of its (i.e., fitness's) absence.'"

Even at the time of the ascertainment of sublation (*bādha*), since the employment of a sentence is impossible without a knowledge of the sentence-meaning qualified by that [sublation] produced through ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*), the knowledge that serves as the basis for the employment of the sentence must be stated to be of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.
For if that too were verbal (*śābda*), it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And thus:
It is entirely inconsistent to say that an inference or similar cognition regarding a certain object has not arisen, while only a verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) regarding it has arisen.

Likewise, the restrictive rule that "it applies only to two specific [types of] cognitions" is also irrelevant; for this reason, he states the following with a sense of dissatisfaction: "In this way, of desire..."
And so forth.

It is not possible for there to be a general state of being an inhibitor—by way of being a certainty regarding the absence of that [object]—with respect to the general class of cognitions of "that which possesses it" (tadvat) which are not produced by worldly sensory contact and are not produced by specific defects. This is because even after a certainty such as "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," [a cognition of the jar may still arise].

For, by the force of the desire "let there arise in me a visual perception having 'jar' as its qualifier and 'ground' as its qualificand," a visual perception would arise with respect to the ground and so forth through the proximity of *upanaya* (mental presentation) regarding the jar and so forth; thus, the charge of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) would be untenable. Rather, [the definition must be qualified].

Furthermore, in the case of visual perception, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator must be stated specifically as the certainty of the absence of that [object], qualified by the absence of a desire to see it; and in the case of inference,
[the relationship holds] by way of being an inference having that as its qualifier.

The relationship between the sublated and the sublator must be postulated by including, as a necessary factor, the state of being qualified by the absence of desire, which consists in the ascertainment of that non-existence;

for it is not admitted that there can be such things as indirect knowledge or imposed (āhārya) cognition. And thus, in the case of verbal cognition, [the role] of the ascertainment of inapplicability...

The meaning is this: one would have to postulate a separate status as an obstructer (*pratibandhakatva*). Rather than that, it is more appropriate to postulate, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), that the cause is simply the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*).

Nor [is there a problem] in the case of inference, where [the cognition of the absence of the reason] occurs through the ascertainment of its absence by way of being a cognition of something other than the perceptible that possesses that [reason].

It should not be argued that because the nature of the obstructive factor (pratibandhakatā) has already been postulated, no further relationship of the obstructed and the obstructor need be postulated in the case of verbal cognition;

for there is no decisive reason (vinigamanāviraha) to determine the qualifier-qualified relationship between the property of being a cognition of the final stage of perception and the property of being a cognition [of the object].

The point is that, because it would result in two instances of the relation between the sublated and the sublator (pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva)— which would be more cumbersome— it is more appropriate to posit a simpler relation by including "verbality" (śābdatva) and "inferentiality" (anumititva) within the delimiting factor of the sublatedness (pratibadhyatāvacchedaka).

Regarding the phrase "the absence of the ascertainment of invalidity": where a cognition common to both doubt and certainty serves as the cause, a doubt regarding the invalidity of that cognition does not obstruct its causal function;
for, through a doubt regarding the invalidity of a cognition, only a doubt regarding the object itself is produced. Thus, even doubt [is a cause].
Therefore, since the certainty of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-niścaya*) itself acts as the disruptor of the causal capacity [of the cognition],
it is precisely the absence of such certainty that constitutes the cause; thus, the absence of certainty alone is included within the defining scope (*avacchedaka-koṭi*) of the causal capacity.
There is complexity because the element of certainty—that [the cognition] must be included—must itself be included.

However, if the certainty of inappropriateness (ayogyatāniścaya) acts as an inhibitor, then even a doubt regarding invalidity (aprāmāṇyasaṃdeha) functions as a factor that disrupts that inhibition; thus, it is simply the general absence of any knowledge of invalidity that is required.

The sense is that there is a parsimony resulting from not including the factor of "certainty" (*niścayatva*) within the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatā*).

Although the inclusion of the factor of certainty is indeed necessary even if the absence of the certainty of incompatibility (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) is taken as the cause by way of its being the absence of such a certainty, nevertheless, provided that it does not have that [incompatibility] as its qualifier...

Compared to the certainty of incompatibility (*ayogyatāniścaya*), which consists in the state of having that absence as its qualifier (*tadabhāvaprakāratva*), there is the certainty of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyaniścayatva*), which consists in the state of having such invalidity as its qualifier (*tādṛśāprāmāṇyaprakārakatva*)— [invalidity] being defined as the state of having that [object] as its qualifier while residing in what lacks it (*tadabhāvavati*).

The point is that it is appropriate to include "the certainty of unfitness" (ayogyatāniścayatva) itself as a factor delimiting the causal capacity (kāraṇatāvacchedaka), due to its greater weight. Regarding the phrase "if the knowledge of fitness [is the cause]," etc.: in the case of verbal cognition such as "the ground possesses a jar," [the absence of such a cognition acts as an obstacle].

The cause is a cognition having the ground as its qualificand and the jar as its qualifier. In that case, the cognition of invalidity is of only one kind: namely, "the cognition has the jar as its qualifier despite the absence of a jar.
Furthermore, there is a cognition of invalidity whose locus is the certainty having the ground as its qualificand and the absence of a jar as its qualifier.

It is of three kinds: (1) that which has the absence of a jar as its qualificandum and the absence of a jar as its qualifier, occurring where there is no absence of a jar; (2) that which has the absence of a jar as its qualificandum and the absence of a jar as its qualifier, occurring where there is a jar; and (3) that which has a jar as its qualifier through the relation of counter-correlativity, occurring in an absence that possesses the absence of a jar through the relation of counter-correlativity. Thus, rather than relying on the inclusion of these three types of knowledge of invalidity, [the definition is formulated differently].

The sense is that simplicity (*lāghava*) consists precisely in the absence of a certainty regarding the invalidity of a single [cognition]. Thus, where the certainty of the absence of that [invalidity] acts as an obstacle,
there the certainty of that which possesses the pervader of its absence [acts as an obstacle], provided it is apprehended as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of that absence.

Since the certainty regarding the property [of being a valid means of knowledge] is not an obstacle, the proponent of the absence of such certainty as a cause must postulate that the absence of the certainty regarding unfitness (*ayogyatva*) is the cause;
however, this need not be postulated by the proponent of the cognition of fitness (*yogyatā*) as the cause.

He states that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because, when any one of those [conditions] such as certainty is present, the exclusion of verbal cognition is possible simply due to the absence of the cause consisting in the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*); thus he says: "just like the certainty of sublation" (*bādhaniścayasyeva*).
Regarding the phrase "in not producing verbal cognition," it refers precisely to the absence of the knowledge of incompatibility (*ayogyatā-jñāna*).

The meaning is: in the view that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) has [the absence of incompatibility] as its cause. The meaning is: at the time of the causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābda-sāmagrī*), when there exists a causal complex constituted by the absence of a certainty regarding incompatibility (*ayogyatā-niścaya*).
"In the absence of the knowledge of compatibility" (*yogyatā-jñāna-abhāva*): [this refers to the aforementioned view].

The meaning is that one must postulate the status of an obstructer (*pratibandhakatva*) for the verbal causal complex (*śābdasāmagrī*)—such as "the ground possesses a jar"—with respect to the mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) of the form "I am devoid of a cognition whose qualifier is another object-entity with respect to a single object-entity.

The underlying intention is that the verbal causal complex is more powerful when its object is distinct [from that of the mental perception]. [The phrase] "it need not be postulated" [refers to this].

The sense is this: when the causal complex for verbal cognition (*śābda-sāmagrī*)—which includes the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā-jñāna*)—is present, the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*) does not arise precisely because its object, namely the absence of that [verbal cognition], is lacking. However, in the case of the absence of the knowledge of semantic competency, there is no causal complex for verbal cognition; thus, the occurrence of such a perception is simply what we desire (*iṣṭāpatti*). || 82 || 83 || Now, [it may be argued]: "In the root text, with that word..."
It was stated that "there is an expectancy for it. However, this alone does not suffice to establish the nature of the cognition of expectancy;
therefore, with this underlying difficulty in mind, he explains:
"the state of being qualified by that word," meaning [the relation] by way of either immediate antecedence or immediate succession, and so forth.

And thus, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for a particular kind of verbal cognition is the state of being a word qualified by another word— connected by either of the aforementioned relations— such that, in the absence of that [first] word, the [second] word lacks the capacity to produce that kind of verbal cognition.

[This is] the state of affairs. Regarding the phrase "and here": when there is the cognition that the word *am* is immediately followed by the word *ghaṭa*, there is no experience of a delay in the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) due to a delay caused by the cognition that the word *am*—in the absence of the word *ghaṭa*—is not productive of a verbal comprehension. Therefore, [the word *am* possesses its own capacity].

Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is simply the state of being immediately preceded by the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*). It is not the case that the inability of the word "is" (*asti*) to produce verbal comprehension in the absence of the cognition of the word "pot" is included in the definition of expectancy; rather, such a statement is made solely for the purpose of specifically identifying the cognitions of words such as "is" and "pot. As for the words "pot" and "objectness" (*karmatva*), however...

The point is that the term *karmatva* (objecthood) does not possess such a nature [of being a non-expresser], because its failure to generate the verbal cognition "the objecthood residing in the pot" is not caused by the absence of the word *ghaṭa*; for even when the word *ghaṭa* is present, it does not generate such a verbal cognition. Now, even so, in a case where a verbal cognition with an established syntactic connection has already been produced...

Furthermore, because there is the undesirable consequence of [the cognition of] verbal meaning arising [from the mere presence of words], he says "or else" (*yadvā*), expressing his dissatisfaction. Regarding the phrase "in its own form alone" (*svarūpata eva*):

the intended meaning is that the knowledge of that [word] is not required for the verbal cognition. Now, it might be argued that the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of words denoting actions and their factors is already accounted for by the condition of contiguity (*āsatti*).
The root [of the objection] is unconnected. This is because we do not accept that "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in proximity in the form of non-intervention.

Rather, as previously admitted, expectancy is the state of one word possessing another word through one of the aforementioned relations; therefore, in order to reconcile that passage, he says: "In this regard... (*atrety*).

Regarding the phrase "immediate succession" (*avyavahitotaratvam*): the sense is that there is no evidence for immediate succession and the like to constitute a relation. Now, one might object: even if the lack of intervention between words constitutes proximity (*āsatti*), the aspect of "succession" (*uttaratva*) must still be accepted as constituting expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). To this, he says: "And succession... and so forth.

And this statement regarding proximity (*āsatti*) as the non-intervention between two words is made according to the view of the ancient masters. However, in the author’s own view, since it is the non-intervention between the cognitions of the two words that constitutes *āsatti*,
and since that [non-intervention] is a cause for verbal comprehension by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), the factor of non-intervention itself—

The Nāstikas do not accept this [view]. However, since the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) can be established simply through the non-intervened knowledge of the words denoting the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), and since there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of those words denoting the action and its factors, it is precisely in that case that the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is of no use. In reality...
It should be noted that, in accordance with the verses of Mauni,
since the cognition of one word while possessing the cognition of another word must be accepted as the nature of *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) hereafter,
it is precisely with this intention that the portion concerning "non-intervention" (*avyavadhāna*) is said to have its purpose fulfilled even in the absence of [actual] contact.

"Let there be the cognition of syntactic connection (anvaya-bodha). This statement was made by adopting the view that the two terms serve as indicators for the specific portion: "the fact that a particular word does not bring about the experience of syntactic connection without another particular word. However, if that portion were also included within the very essence of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), then it would exist in its own right.

It should be noted that this undesirable consequence does not arise because, as a cause of verbal comprehension, the word *rāja-* (king) generates a comprehension of the relation (*anvaya*) when combined with the word *putra* (son), even in the absence of the word *puruṣa* (man).
In the root text, "ayi," etc.: when the speaker intends to convey the relationship between the son and the king, [the cognition arises] through the son...

There is a simultaneous comprehension of the connection with the referent of the word *rājan* (king). However, when the speaker intends to convey the relation between the man (*puruṣa*) and the king, then there occurs a comprehension of the connection between the man and the king alone.
Thus, it is intention (*tātparya*) itself that determines whether the comprehension occurs through the son or through the man.

The sense is that there is no restrictive factor [to determine the meaning] once expectancy has arisen. Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu" (but surely): "knowledge of the speaker's intention" means the knowledge of the speaker's desire, namely, "May there be an understanding of the king's relation to both the man and the son. "Certainty regarding syntactic unity" refers to the word "rājñaḥ" (of the king).

The collective meaning is as follows: it is the time of the ascertainment that [the word] was uttered with the intention of conveying a connection with the referent of the word *putra* (son), and not with the intention of conveying a connection with the referent of the word *puruṣa* (man). He states another opinion: "The co-occurrence [of words] does not constitute the body of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)."

And so forth. "Precisely because it is the cause" means that the cognition of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-jñāna*)—in the form of the cognition that "let there be a cognition of the relation between the king and the man"—is not the cause of verbal comprehension; this is the sense. "Of the aforementioned co-utterance" refers to the previously mentioned syntactic collocation.
The meaning is: the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), which consists of a desire in the form "let this word produce a cognition of syntactic connection with that word.

Regarding the phrase "the definition of expectancy": the definition of expectancy is that one word possesses another word by means of the relation of being immediately followed by it; such is the meaning of "the definition of expectancy."

"Having that word as its object of knowledge" (*tatpadajñānaparam*) means that the state of possessing the cognition of that word (*tatpadajñānavattva*), through the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitotaratva*), is itself the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). The point is that otherwise, since words are absent in the poetry of the mute, expectancy would be untenable. "In comparison with all [other factors]" (*sarvāpekṣayā*).
The meaning is "with regard to the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) and so forth. The intention is that one must assume the connection of the word heard in those [preceding] passages.
Regarding the phrase "the lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) and so on: a lion, having gone out from its own den and traveled a great distance, returns once again...
Just as one turns back and looks at one's own house, so too in certain subsequent sentences there is no connection with a preceding word;
when a preceding word is connected to a subsequent sentence, that is *siṃhāvalokana* (the lion’s glance). [This occurs] in one place among the subsequent sentences.

The connection of the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) with one [element], its lack of connection [with another], and then its connection again in a subsequent sentence—this is the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). It should be understood that there is a distinction between cases where the preceding word connects sequentially with all subsequent sentences, as in the example of the "Ganges stream" (*gaṅgāsrotas*), and those where it does not. Now, regarding the root text:

It has been established that the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) constitutes the *tātparya* [of a sentence]. It must be stated that the knowledge of that [intention] is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). In that regard, in a situation where two sentences—"Bring the jar" and "Bring the cloth"—are employed, since there is knowledge of two intentions on the part of the speaker, from which sentence does the comprehension of what kind of meaning arise?
Since it is impossible to determine [the speaker's intention] otherwise, he shows the form of the knowledge of that intention with the words "by such a desire.

Thus, when there arises a knowledge of the speaker’s intention— consisting of a desire whose qualificandum is a particular sentence through the relation of being uttered by one whom [the hearer] himself employs— that [knowledge] serves as the cause for the verbal cognition produced by that same sentence.

The meaning is that there is no fixed rule regarding the cause. In that context, "at one time" means that sometimes the intended object of the speaker's purpose (*tātparya*) is the meaning "a white-colored dog is running," while at other times the intended object of the purpose is the meaning "a black dog is running this way. This applies to both cases as well.

And this was stated on the basis of not accepting the rule that "a word uttered once conveys its meaning only once"; otherwise, it should be understood that this was said with the intention of repeating the word *saindhava*. [This refers to] the phrase "that which is doubted," etc.

The meaning is that it has been stated in the *Cintāmaṇi* that "that which, when there is doubt about it or certainty regarding its absence, acts as an obstacle to the arising [of the knowledge] of something—certainty regarding that is the cause of that [knowledge]; in the case of inference, this is nothing other than pervasion (*vyāpti*). Here, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) means proximity; separation (*viyoga*) means distance; and coexistence (*sāhacarya*) means residing in the same locus.

In such cases as "The jar is to be removed," the apprehension of the speaker's intention (tātparya) regarding a nearby jar arises due to proximity. In such cases as "Bring the jar here," the apprehension of the speaker's intention regarding a distant jar arises due to distance. In such cases as "Bring the jar and the cloth," [the apprehension of the intention regarding both arises from the context].

The apprehension of the intention (*tātparya*) regarding the jar and the cloth within the words "jar" and "cloth"—which function in a single location—is due to their association (*sāhacarya*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [states such as] being face-to-face are included. [The phrase] "by virtue of having an established necessity of occurring immediately prior" [is used] because even for one who maintains that the knowledge of intention is a cause [of verbal comprehension], it is precisely for the sake of the knowledge of intention [that this is required].

The point is that prior to the arising of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), contextual factors (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth must necessarily be admitted [as causes].
