[The phrase] "there is no possibility of being a cause" means that, by including the property of "immediately following that specific [cause]" within the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the effectness of that specific effect, any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is excluded.
The sense is that there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress of causes and effects.

"Due to the absence of a teacher" means due to the absence of a teacher other than God; thus, in the absence of a teacher, there would be an absence of knowledge of the sentences constituting the Vedas.

Even if there is an impossibility of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), there is no harm. It was stated in the root text that the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is taught by scripture (*āgama*); however, that is incorrect, because the Great Dissolution is not established by scripture. By such scriptural passages as "As before, Dhātṛ fashioned [the world]," only the partial dissolution (*khaṇḍapralaya*) is indicated.

Because it has been indicated [by scripture]. For this very reason, even the dispute regarding the "great dissolution" (mahāpralaya) becomes consistent, since no dispute is possible regarding what is established by authoritative scripture (āgama). Therefore, he states that the word *pralaya* refers to a partial dissolution (*khaṇḍapralaya*)—namely, "of the effect-substance" (*kāryadravya*) and "having the effect as its locus" (*kāryādhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is "having as its locus an effect whose nature is the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth.

Although it would have been more appropriate to state simply that it has substance as its locus for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it was not stated thus because there is a lack of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its subsistence in eternal substances during the dissolution (*pralaya*). Nor is it the case that...
It should be stated that the very impossibility of eternal substances possessing a form of permanence characterized by being everlasting is the proof in this case;
for permanence consists precisely in not being the counter-positive of either destruction or prior non-existence.
The point is that the existence of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) during the period of dissolution is established by the fact that otherwise a subsequent creation would be impossible.

In the scripture, the meaning of the word "space" (*nabhas*) is indeed the world of the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) and so forth, because space is eternal. Likewise, the meaning of the word "darkness" (*tamas*) is merely limited darkness, because darkness, being of the nature of the absence of light, is eternal. [Objection: But is it not said that...?

In the case of the statement of Śuka, "He sprinkles," etc., the knowledge of the intention (tātparya) residing in God is not the cause [of verbal comprehension], because it would follow that God’s will could be deceptive. Thus, the root text's claim that even in the statement of Śuka, the knowledge of God’s intention is the cause, is inconsistent. In such a statement by Śuka...

Since the knowledge of intention (*tātparya*) is not a cause [of verbal cognition], he states "consistent" (*saṃvādī*) for that purpose. This means "that which produces valid cognition. Furthermore, in the case of the verbal cognition produced by the sentence of a parrot, "He sprinkles with fire," the knowledge of God's intention is not a cause, because God...
Because the desire of one who speaks falsely would [otherwise] be [considered *tātparya*], this was stated in order to exclude such sentences. Nor should it be argued:

"Since *tātparya* is the nature of the speaker's intention, and since God lacks the status of being the speaker of the parrot's words, how can God's desire constitute *tātparya*? For [the definition applies] only to one who possesses an effort conducive to the sentence.

The sense is that, because the effort of God (īśvara-prayatna) is conducive to all effects by virtue of being the agency of a speaker, it is also conducive to the speech of a parrot; the sense is that, since there is an absence of intention on the part of the parrot, one must—having no other recourse—accept God alone as the speaker. [This is repeated: because of the absence of intention on the part of the parrot.
It should be understood that this is because, having no other recourse, the speakerhood must be attributed to God alone.

Likewise, it should be recognized that even the intention of the instructor—through the effort of teaching in a manner consistent with the parrot’s words—constitutes the *tātparya* (intentional meaning). This applies in all cases where multiple meanings are possible.
With the intention that it would be inconsistent [to say] "in some cases" because the knowledge of *tātparya* (speaker's intention) is accepted as the cause [of verbal comprehension],
he provides an explanation of that very phrase "in some cases" by saying "in the case of words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*). Now,
if "having multiple meanings" means "having multiple powers (*śakti*"), then [the definition would fail] in the case of words used metaphorically (*lākṣaṇika*) for multiple meanings.
Since it might otherwise follow that there would be no restriction regarding the intention to convey a specific meaning for a certain word at a certain time,
he states— beginning with "gṛhīta"— that polysemy consists precisely in a word having multiple meanings grasped as its denotations.

The inclusion of the word "gṛhīta" (grasped) is intended to exclude words such as "hari," which, despite having multiple meanings, [are restricted] when they refer to only one specific meaning on a particular occasion.

At that time, since the comprehension of meaning through verbal cognition is possible by means of the apprehension of expressive power (*śakti*) alone, the knowledge of intention (*tātparya*) is not mentioned as a regulator of verbal cognition; this is because it is more extensive than the assumption of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which occurs when multiple meanings have been apprehended. The phrase "distinct meanings" refers to [the case where] in a single [word], there is...

"Of one whose power has been grasped" means of one for whom the indication (lakṣaṇā) has been grasped with respect to another meaning. To the question, "What is to be included by the word 'etcetera' (ādi)? he says: "By 'etcetera'. Nor is it the case that because the relation to the primary meaning itself constitutes the indication, the knowledge of the primary power (śakti) is necessarily required for the knowledge of the indication.

And thus, it should not be said that this [statement] is redundant because its meaning is already covered by the previously mentioned phrase "of one who has grasped the denotative power (śakti) or indication (lakṣaṇā) for distinct meanings. This is because the compound *vibhinnārtha* is to be analyzed as a bahuvrīhi ending in a plural: "one whose denotative power or indication has been grasped (*gṛhītā*) with respect to various distinct meanings (*vibhinnārtheṣu*)," thereby referring to one who has grasped the denotative power for multiple meanings.
Because a word whose specific definition has been grasped constitutes the meaning of the preceding sentence.

He states the meaning of the term *mīmāṃsā*: "Reasoning (*tarka*) consists of the cognition of parsimony (*lāghava*). In the case of the injunction "One should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds," it is determined that the plural number refers specifically to the number three, due to the parsimony of being the first [number] to present itself.

Now, if it is asked: "If the word *pariśodhita* has the meaning 'accompanied by,' then what is the other *tarka* accompanied by the *tarka* of parsimony (*lāghava*)? he says: "*Tarka* is inference. And the form of that inference is as follows:

The meaning of the plural number in the word *kapiñjalān* (partridges) consists of three or more, because it is denoted by the plural suffix; in this regard, the cognition of parsimony (*lāghava*) serves as a cooperative factor, since numbers such as four and so on are also denotable by the plural suffix. Thus, in the case of the Veda, the determination of the meaning occurs through the lack of [prior] knowledge regarding the intended sense (*tātparya*).

Thus [it is said]. "In other cases, there is more" means that since verbal cognition is not experienced in instances where there is doubt regarding the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) and so forth, it follows that the knowledge of the speaker's intention is necessarily a cause for verbal cognition in general; this is the sense. || 84 || Thus.
The Wave on Sound in the *Dinakarī-taraṅgiṇī*, a commentary on the *Muktāvalī-prakāśa* composed by Śrī Rāmarudra Bhaṭṭācārya, is completed.
